letters of the Sefer Torah and Jewish souls

title.en: Each Jew's letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav recalls that every Jew draws from a letter of the Sefer Torah, which explains differences among people. Some tzaddikim, like the Chofetz Chaim, are beyond imitation because their letter is especially holy, and a tzaddik who put all his strength into Shabbos had his root in Shabbos.

title.en: Families, neighborhoods and sedras

summary.en: The Rav explains that a family is people whose letters form one word, three families make a neighborhood like a column, and a community is like a sedra. Each Shabbos is woven from its own sedra, so the Zohar forbids mixing sedras, and the five sefarim mirror the camps in the Midbar.

title.en: Why sedras are sometimes joined

summary.en: The Rav asks how two sedras can ever be read together if mixing them is forbidden. He explains that each group of Jews has its own Shabbos, customs and even halachos, as with Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, yet at certain times unity must be demonstrated, as the shevatim gathered in Yerushalayim on Yom Tov.

title.en: Four seasons of ahavas chinam

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Beis Hamikdash was destroyed for sinas chinam, so at four times of year the sedras are joined to show ahavas chinam: before Nisan and Tishrei, the two months of hoped-for redemption, in the Three Weeks, and in Sefirah. He then asks why in a leap year the Sefirah sedras are not joined, rejecting the answer that it is only because of the extra weeks.

title.en: Chassidim and misnagdim: shlishi and shishi

summary.en: The Rav describes the separations of recent generations, Chassidim and misnagdim, Ashkenazim and Sefardim, and how halacha governs every movement, as the Chasam Sofer's father taught his son. He illustrates with the aliyah given to a Rav: shlishi by halacha, shishi among Chassidim following the Zohar, and on weeks of joined sedras shlishi and shishi come together.

title.en: The Yam Suf and the quarrel of shlishi and shishi

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the sea refused to split for Moshe, since the sea was created on the third day and man on the sixth, until it saw Yosef's coffin. Hashem rebuked the sea for quarreling over shlishi and shishi while Jews were in danger, and the Rav applies this to today's machlokes, which comes from jealousy.

title.en: Kinah through history and its root

summary.en: The Rav shows that kinah breeds sinah, from the nations' hatred of Jews to the nachash, Kayin, Yosef's brothers, Yeravam and Kamtza bar Kamtza, and tells of a tzaddik who traveled to Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz to learn freedom from kinah. He traces kinah to the moon's complaint against the sun.

title.en: Mashiach, the moon and Yehuda and Ephraim

summary.en: The Rav brings Yeshayahu's vision of peace among animals and the verse that Ephraim will not envy Yehuda, explaining that the moon will be restored. He lists three expressions of the moon's diminution, including its slower pace that requires a leap month, and identifies Yehuda and David with the moon.

title.en: David and Yehonasan and Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: The Rav presents the love of Yehonasan for David despite Shaul's jealousy as a symbol of the end of kinah, which each month is hinted in Kiddush Levana and the haftarah of Machar Chodesh. He explains the Rosh Chodesh chatas 'for Hashem' as the promise of the moon's repair, and says the machlokes among Jews holds back Mashiach.

title.en: The leap year answer and closing

summary.en: The Rav answers his question: a leap year, when the moon catches up with the sun, is itself a sign of the moon's repair, so Sefirah needs no combined sedras. He closes with Rosh Chodesh Iyar as a month of Torah, calls to erase kinah, since a Jew's deeds register in all creation like a switchboard, and expresses hope for Mashiach.

catalogTitle: סעודת ר”ח ניסן לאברכי אמ”י: DIGITAL ELECTRONICS הנסיון המיוחד שלנו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that before Mashiach the Jewish people pass through a series of refining tests, that electronics are the test of today's generation, and that Nissan and Pesach give every Jew the power to renew himself and walk out of it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nissan as a time of renewal: Adam was created in Nissan, and each day of the dedication of the Nesi'im was a renewal, which the Ba'al Shem Tov tied to the thirteenth gate that includes all the tribes. He then brings Daniel's prophecy that before the end many will be sifted, whitened and refined like silver. These refinings, he says, began about three hundred years ago: Shabbetai Tzvi, the Frankists, Reform in Germany, the emptiness of early America, Communism and Zionism, each of which tore away multitudes. Today's test is electronics, an addiction like alcoholism whose core desire is immorality and which removes the taste of davening, learning and the Seder. Yet every Jew can leave Mitzrayim and become a new person in Nissan, when all of nature is renewed. The Rav calls for a firm 'no', throwing out the devices with the chametz, and binding oneself to Hashem through Pesach.

en: Nissan is a time when a Jew must renew himself like a newborn child, because Adam was actually created in Nissan.
Before Mashiach the Jewish people go through refinings, as Daniel says that many will be sifted, whitened and refined like silver in a furnace.
The refinings began about three hundred years ago with Shabbetai Tzvi and continued through the Frankists, Reform, Communism and Zionism, each of which tore away multitudes of Jews.
The test of today's generation is electronics, an addiction like alcoholism that takes away the taste of davening, learning and the Seder; it is probably the last test before Mashiach.
Even one caught in it can get out, because every Jew can leave Mitzrayim and become a new person in Nissan.
The Rav calls for a strong 'no' to the yetzer hara: throwing out the devices together with the chametz, since chametz and matzah cannot exist together.
Pesach, unlike Shavuos and Sukkos, carries kares, because it is the point of emunah and of tearing oneself free, and whoever keeps it binds himself to Hashem.

title.en: Nissan, the Nesi'im and the thirteenth gate

summary.en: The Rav opens with Nissan as a month of renewal, when Adam was created and a Jew should become like a newborn. He describes each day of the dedication of the Nesi'im as a renewal and explains why the Ba'al Shem Tov's followers did not say the siddur's prayer about one's own tribe: today every Jew belongs to the thirteenth gate that includes all the tribes.

title.en: Daniel's prophecy of the refinings

summary.en: The Rav calls Pesach bright days to be used, citing his rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz. He then explains that before Mashiach there will be tests to determine who merits the redemption, bringing the end of Daniel that many will be sifted, whitened and refined like silver in a furnace.

title.en: Three hundred years of refining

summary.en: The Rav traces the refinings of the last three hundred years: Shabbetai Tzvi, the Frankists, and Reform, which destroyed German Jewry as the Meshech Chochmah foresaw. He connects this to the 'book' in Daniel and Malachi in which those who stay loyal are written, and describes the early immigrants in America who lost their children.

title.en: Communism and Zionism

summary.en: The Rav describes Communism, which emptied the great chassidic centers of Russia within seventy years and was the first kingdom of heresy, as the Gemara at the end of Sotah foretells. He then describes Zionism, which taught that a land and a language make a Jew; both movements have collapsed, but the destruction they left remains.

title.en: Electronics, today's test

summary.en: The Rav calls electronics the test of today's generation. From what people tell him as mashgiach, he describes it as an addiction like alcoholism, whose core desire is immorality, which takes away the taste of davening, Gemara and the Seder. He says it is probably the last test before Mashiach and that knowing this can help one save others.

title.en: Every Jew can leave Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that one sunk in these desires cannot praise Hashem with kedushah, and brings the end of the parsha of tzitzis: 'you shall be holy', 'I am Hashem who took you out of Mitzrayim'. Every Jew can leave Mitzrayim and must show himself as having left it. Today's test also includes hester panim, so it all rests on emunah and on holding onto the mitzvos of Pesach.

title.en: A new people, a renewed nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that at the Exodus the Jews became a new people and that every Jew becomes a Jew through it, citing the Maharal. This renewal comes down into nature: the blessing over the blossoming trees, the haftarah of the dry bones on Pesach, and the spring described in Shir HaShirim. When all of nature is renewed, a Jew should not be the exception.

title.en: The drunkard, and throwing out the chametz

summary.en: The Rav tells of a drunkard who held back for three days and then rewarded himself with a drink, and draws from it the need for one strong 'no'. He calls to throw out the devices together with the chametz, the true spiritual chametz, since chametz and matzah cannot coexist, and describes Pesach as the time when everything becomes new.

title.en: Why Pesach carries kares

summary.en: Citing the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav explains that although Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, only Pesach carries kares, like milah, because it is the point of emunah and of Avraham Avinu; whoever keeps it becomes bound to Hashem. He closes with the hope that the treasured people bind themselves to Hashem, and with l'chaim and wishes for a kosher and happy Pesach.

catalogTitle: אסון בברא פארק: דברי חיזוק אחר האסון בבארא פארק

oneLiner.en: After the tragedy in Boro Park, the Rav shows from Pinchas's zealotry, done as one of Klal Yisrael, how the Jewish people revealed their true holiness this week, and strengthens them with emunah in hashgachah pratis and the comfort of Parshas Pinchas.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Pinchas, who received the kehunah only through his zealotry, and asks what the Torah means by saying he was zealous 'in their midst'. He explains that Pinchas did not act as someone above Klal Yisrael but as a simple member of it, showing that the Jewish people are holy and separate from Zimri, whom he describes as a Jew with a foreign growth attached to him. This week, he says, a Jew became such a Zimri, while thousands of Jews in Boro Park searched all night and the levayah was a great kiddush Hashem, showing the signs of the Jewish people: merciful, bashful and doers of kindness. He then explains that Parshas Pinchas is a comfort, with Eliyahu and the festivals, and that this rare year it falls outside the Three Weeks by hashgachah. He reads from Tzafun Lashomer Emunim on believing that everything is guided by Hashem, and closes by calling to receive Shabbos with joy.

en: Pinchas was zealous 'in their midst': not as someone above Klal Yisrael but as a simple member of it, to show that the Jewish people are holy.
Zimri was a Jew to whom a foreign growth had attached itself, and this week a Jew became such a Zimri.
The thousands who searched all night and the levayah revealed the signs of the Jewish people: merciful, bashful and doers of kindness.
Parshas Pinchas is a comfort, and this year it falls outside the Three Weeks by hashgachah, so that Jews have comfort after this week's tragedy.
Everything that happens is guided by Hashem; when Mashiach comes it will be understood, and now one must believe that it was all for good.

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pinchas received the kehunah only through his zealotry, knowing he might lose it, and asks what 'in their midst' means. He answers that Pinchas acted not as someone higher than Klal Yisrael but as a simple Jew among them, to show that the Jewish people are holy.

title.en: A Zimri this week, and Klal Yisrael's response

summary.en: The Rav describes Zimri as a Jew to whom a foreign growth attached itself, and says that this week a Jew became such a Zimri. Against this, thousands of Jews from Boro Park and elsewhere searched all night, the levayah was a great kiddush Hashem, and the Jewish people showed they are merciful, bashful and doers of kindness.

title.en: Parshas Pinchas as comfort, by hashgachah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Parshas Pinchas, with Eliyahu, the korbanos and the festivals, is a comfort in the Three Weeks, and that this rare year it falls outside them, with the haftarah of Eliyahu. Nothing is by chance; the tragedy is part of the tikkun of souls that will be understood when Mashiach comes, and now one must believe it was for good.

title.en: Emunah in hashgachah, and comfort through Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav reads from the Tzafun Lashomer Emunim a text on the principles of faith: that Hashem is good and merciful and everything, even the suffering of tzaddikim, is guided by Him. He returns to the beauty of Klal Yisrael shown this week, and closes that one must be strengthened and comforted by Shabbos and receive it with joy.

catalogTitle: הכרת הטוב: נודה לך ונספר

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that hod, thanks and self-effacement, is the root of a Jew, from Modeh Ani each morning to the Korban Pesach, and that this power belongs most of all to the lowest souls whom Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai lifts up.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the six hundred thousand letters of the Torah that match the six hundred thousand souls: the first letters are Moshe, David and Moshiach, the last ones the lowest souls of the generations before Moshiach. Souls are also ordered by the middos, and ours are of hod, the lowest; hod shebehod is Lag BaOmer, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who sees the hidden worth of even the lowest Jew. Hod means beauty, thanks and submission. Leah thanked Hashem at Yehudah's birth for receiving more than her share, so kingship, which demands that the king stay small, went to Yehudah. A Jew's first word each day is Modeh Ani, and the Korban Pesach, the first offering, is a thanks offering of pure kindness. Modeh Ani is said with impure hands to declare that the kelipah is nothing, as Avraham did with dust. The Rav ends with Pesach Sheini, the Alter Rebbe's day and thanks for the final redemption.

en: The souls of the last generations are souls of hod, the lowest level, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose day is hod shebehod, reveals the hidden worth in them.
Hod means beauty, thanks and submission; Leah's thanks at Yehudah's birth came from feeling she had received more than her share.
Kingship belongs to Yehudah because a king must hold himself no higher than the lowest Jew, and only one rooted in thanks can do so.
A Jew's first word each morning, Modeh Ani, sets the tone of the whole day, since everything follows its beginning.
The Korban Pesach, the first offering of the Jewish people, is a thanks offering for a redemption that came through Hashem's kindness and not through their deeds.
Modeh Ani is said even with impure hands to declare that the kelipah has no power before Hashem, and through this declaration it is nullified.

title.en: Souls of hod and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

summary.en: The Rav matches the letters of the Torah to the souls, from Moshe, David and Moshiach at the start to the lowest souls at the end, and explains that our souls are of hod. Hod shebehod is Lag BaOmer, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who sees and reveals the hidden worth of the lowest Jews.

title.en: Hod as thanks: Leah and Yehudah

summary.en: The Rav lists the meanings of hod: beauty, thanks and submission. He brings Leah's words at Yehudah's birth and Rashi's explanation that she received more than her share, and explains that a Jew who knows everything is a gift bows in thanks, as at Modim.

title.en: Why kingship belongs to Yehudah; Modeh Ani

summary.en: The Rav explains that a king must not hold himself above his brothers, which is why kingship was given to Yehudah, born of Leah's thanks, and he brings David who stayed small. Since everything follows its beginning, a Jew's first word, Modeh Ani, must leave its mark on the whole day; this is why a Jew is called Yehudi.

title.en: The Korban Pesach as a thanks offering

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Exodus came not by merit but because the Jews are Hashem's children, so the first offering, the Korban Pesach, is a thanks offering. He brings the Abarbanel's question why it has no chametz loaves, and answers that it is an offering of pure kindness, not of deeds.

title.en: Modeh Ani with impure hands

summary.en: The Rav brings the Hayom Yom that Modeh Ani is said before washing, and asks why one does not wash first. He explains that declaring the world nothing before Hashem nullifies evil, as in bittul chametz and Avraham's dust against the kings, and brings the Gemara in Shabbos about the 'king's daughter' on the fingers who insists on proper washing.

title.en: The true prince and Pesach Sheini

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the proud 'king's daughter' of the kelipah with the Jew, a true king's son who makes himself small; his Modeh Ani with impure hands nullifies her. He then explains Pesach Sheini: the impure argued that the Korban Pesach, like Modeh Ani, could be brought in impurity, and it was instead set in the week of hod to show that even the lowest souls bring it.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe's day and closing thanks

summary.en: The Rav brings a teaching linking the twenty-fourth of Teves to Lag BaOmer, and explains that the Alter Rebbe and his successors continued Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's work of raising the lowest Jew through shluchim. He closes with thanks to Hashem, mentions birthdays being marked, his own among them, and wishes for the final redemption.

catalogTitle: Every Jew is A Letter in the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that when Moshe Rabbeinu counted the Jews 'by the number of names' he was counting the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah, so that every Jew is a letter in the Torah and the camp in the desert was itself a Sefer Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling the Shabbos before Shavuos the aufruf before the chuppah of Matan Torah, and turns to Parshas Bamidbar. He asks why Moshe, Aharon and the Nesi'im had to count the Jews themselves, and what 'counting names' means. Bringing the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim, he explains that the 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah: each letter carries countless halachos and secrets, and a letter that is counted is never nullified. Counting by names joins each Jew's individuality to the whole, and only leaders who know each neshama can do it. The arrangement of the camps is the arranging of the letters into a Torah; Shevet Levi, counted apart, are the 22 root letters, which is why so many teachers of Torah are Kohanim and Levi'im. The megadef was evicted because an extra letter makes a Sefer Torah pasul. He closes with stories and practical words on preparing for Shavuos, when the Torah is given anew.

en: The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf before the wedding of Matan Torah, where Har Sinai held over the people was the chuppah.
Every Jew is a letter, or part of a letter, in the Sefer Torah; there are 600,000 letters for 600,000 neshamos, and if one is missing the Torah is pasul.
Counting 'by the number of names' joins each Jew's individuality to his place in the whole, so only leaders like Moshe and Aharon, who know the secrets of each neshama, could do the counting.
Setting up the camps under flags is arranging the letters into words and pesukim, and Shevet Levi, counted separately, are the roots of the letters, the teachers of Klal Yisrael.
Every Shavuos the Torah is given anew, so one must prepare for it as for a Rosh Hashanah of Torah and not sleep through the davening and the reading.

title.en: The aufruf Shabbos before Matan Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Shabbos before Yom Tov holds the bounty of the Yom Tov, and brings the haftarah's image of Klal Yisrael as Hashem's bride, bound by emunah. Matan Torah was the wedding with Har Sinai as the chuppah, so this Shabbos is the aufruf, built from the sedra that is read on it.

title.en: Why Moshe himself counted the people

summary.en: The Rav goes through the counting at the start of Bamidbar and contrasts it with the American census taker of his youth, an unemployed man sent door to door. He asks why Moshe, Aharon and the Nesi'im had to spend their time counting, and notes the repetition: a count, the Levi'im, the four camps under flags, and a recount with the same total.

title.en: Counting names; every Jew a letter

summary.en: The Rav asks what 'bemispar shemos', counting names, means, and brings the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters of the Torah, which he calls an understatement. He brings that there are 600,000 Jews like the 600,000 letters, several Jews sometimes making up one letter, and describes a scratched letter that stops the reading and renders the Sefer Torah pasul.

title.en: A letter that is never nullified

summary.en: The Rav says every person present is at least part of a letter in the Sefer Torah, and that each letter carries countless halachos and secrets. The sages were called soferim because for them each letter was a davar shebeminyan, a counted thing that is never nullified, as a drop of milk is in sixty parts of soup; he ends with the sefarim's reading of the name Yisrael as the 600,000 letters.

title.en: Names, not numbers: the eyes of the congregation

summary.en: The Rav explains that a census turns people into numbers while a family calls each child by a name that tells the secret of his neshama, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim on the prophecy given to parents at naming. Moshe's count joined the name to the number, so only leaders who know each neshama's secrets, past and future, could count; they are the 'eyes of the congregation' who see the inner glow of every Jew.

title.en: Arranging the letters into camps

summary.en: Recalling that the Aseres HaDibros contain the whole Torah, the Rav explains that once the 600,000 letters were counted they had to be arranged into words and pesukim, like letters that must not be spilled on paper; this is the command to camp under flags. The five camps match the five Chumashim, with the Kohanim and Levi'im in the center as Vayikra, Toras Kohanim, is the middle Chumash, and he raises that Shevet Levi was counted separately.

title.en: Kohanim and Levi'im, the root letters

summary.en: The Rav points to an open miracle: Moshe's blessing that Levi will teach Torah to Yaakov is visible in the many Kohanim and Levi'im among the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch and the leading roshei yeshiva, far beyond their tenth of a congregation. Shevet Levi are the roots of the neshamos, and their count of 22,000 corresponds to the 22 letters of the aleph-beis that are the roots of the 600,000 letters.

title.en: The megadef and the camp as a Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the episode of the man who claimed a place in the camp of Dan, lost the din Torah, cursed and was put to death, and asks why they cared in so vast a desert. He answers that the camp was Hashem's Sefer Torah, each word a family and each line a neighborhood, so an extra letter would make it pasul; he adds that the many colored flags show Klal Yisrael is many colors yet one.

title.en: Shavuos, when the Torah is given anew

summary.en: The Rav says nothing requires as much preparation as Shavuos, since the Torah is given anew each year, and tells how Reb Yechezkel Shinever went to Belz for Shavuos to see the thunder and lightning of Sinai until his father, the Sanzer Rav, showed it to him at home. He compares Shavuos to Rosh Hashanah, brings a tzaddik who feared Shavuos more, and tells of the Bluzhever Rebbe, whose heart beat irregularly six days before receiving the Torah.

title.en: Don't sleep through the wedding

summary.en: The Rav criticizes those who stay up all night and then doze through the davening and the Aseres HaDibros, when each Jew receives his portion in the Torah, comparing them to a chassan who sleeps through his own chuppah, and says those who cannot manage should rest a few hours first, especially for Musaf. He closes with a tzaddik's teaching that even one who missed the fifty days can recount them until the last moment of the seventh week.

catalogTitle: המצב ב: התעוררי! התעוררי!

oneLiner.en: Faced with the Iranian threat to destroy the Jewish people, the Rav calls on Jews to wake up from their indifference and answer the danger with teshuvah, tefillah, Torah, chessed and unity, trusting that Hashem's evident miracles point toward salvation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam in Hilchos Taaniyos: it is a mitzvah to cry out to Hashem in every communal trouble, and treating a trouble as mere chance is cruelty that brings further troubles. He then describes the present danger: the leader of Iran openly threatens to kill every Jew, like Haman, and seeks a nuclear bomb, yet people stay silent and busy with trivialities. Without panic, he reads the Pesikta Rabbasi on the kings of Persia and Arabia provoking each other before Mashiach's coming, noting how closely it resembles the present. He points to the miracles Hashem has shown in Eretz Yisrael, and learns from Manoach's wife that such wonders signal salvation, but, citing Rav Tzadok on Eliyahu, insists one must still pray. He calls for Torah, chessed and tefillah, undisturbed learning, special prayers, and above all unity, as in the days of Haman.

en: According to the Rambam, crying out to Hashem in a communal trouble is a mitzvah and part of the path of teshuvah, and calling the trouble mere chance is cruelty that brings more troubles.
The Rav says the Iranian leader's open threat to kill every Jew is a terrible danger, and the general silence and indifference toward it is a great wrong.
The miracles Hashem has shown in Eretz Yisrael are, like the wonders Manoach and his wife saw, a sign that Hashem intends salvation and not harm.
Even with Hashem's assurance of salvation, one must still pray and do teshuvah, as Rav Tzadok learns from Eliyahu praying for the rain he had been promised.
To be saved from the birth pangs of Mashiach one must strengthen Torah and chessed, with fixed, intense learning that is not interrupted by the telephone.
Haman's decree was annulled through the gathering and unity of all the Jews, and the Rav calls for the same love and unity now, approaching Shabbos Shekalim and Adar.

title.en: The Iranian threat and the silence

summary.en: The Rav describes the Iranian leader's declared intent to kill every Jew and his pursuit of a nuclear bomb, and asks why people stay silent and indifferent instead of crying out and praying. He tells of his request for a gathering and of Rav Rosenblum's words that this is a time of judgment for the whole community and every individual.

title.en: Persia and Arabia in the Pesikta

summary.en: The Rav says there is no cause for panic and reads the Pesikta Rabbasi about the year of Mashiach's revelation, when the king of Persia provokes the king of Arabia and Hashem tells Yisrael that the time of redemption has come. With the Gemara on Edom and Paras and the Maharal linking Paras to Yishmael, he notes the striking resemblance to today, while saying no one can know for sure.

title.en: Miracles as a sign, yet prayer is needed

summary.en: The Rav describes the miracles in Eretz Yisrael, where missiles fall and almost no one is hurt, and learns from Manoach's wife that such wonders show Hashem intends salvation. Yet, citing Rav Tzadok on Eliyahu and a Midrash on the wall of water at the Yam Suf, he insists that even with a promise one must pray and do teshuvah.

title.en: Torah and chessed against chevlei Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin that Torah and gemilus chasadim save from the birth pangs of Mashiach, and the passuk in Tzefanyah, and calls for prayer, a cheshbon hanefesh and fixed, fiery learning. He explains that learning is like Shabbos, so the phone should not interrupt it and the beis medrash must not become a marketplace.

title.en: Unity against Haman, then and now

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman's decree was annulled through the unity of all the Jews, recommends specific prayers, including the kapitel Tehillim the Belzer Rav instituted against wars, and cites the Gemara to pray before trouble comes. Through the half shekel and Korach's dispute he teaches that unity is the remedy, and closes with a call to approach Shabbos Shekalim and Adar with joy and bitachon.

catalogTitle: סיום השס: סיום השס בבית מדרש אמונת ישראל בביתר

oneLiner.en: At a siyum haShas, the Rav explains from the Ba'al HaTanya and the Midrash that every member of a group that finishes Shas together shares in the whole Shas and in its 'kingship', and asks that the merit of Torah learning bring the redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav calls it a great privilege to join a group in Eretz Yisroel completing Shas. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's request at the end of the Tanya that every town divide the masechtos each year and finish Shas, small minyanim joining a larger one. From this he learns that each member is connected to the whole Shas, as the Lubavitcher Rebbe explains, through the bond of souls among them. He brings the Midrash on 'sixty are the queens', the sixty masechtos, and explains that whoever learns a masechta, or even halachah after halachah, merits a share of 'malchus'. Turning to the present, he says the situation grows sharper and Jews need a great salvation; when Jews in Eretz Yisroel and abroad learn and daven for each other, their tefillos join through Yerushalayim. He mentions the Midrash that learning Mishnah among the nations brings the ingathering of exiles, and closes with a prayer for the great nechamah.

en: The Ba'al HaTanya asks that every town divide the masechtos each year and complete Shas, and that small minyanim join a larger one to do it.
In a group that finishes Shas, each member is connected to the whole Shas and is counted as having finished it, through the bond of souls among them.
Based on the Midrash on 'sixty are the queens', whoever learns a masechta, or even one halachah after another, gains a share in 'malchus'.
Jews today need a great salvation, and when Jews in Eretz Yisroel and abroad learn and daven for one another their tefillos are joined together through Yerushalayim.
The merit of Jews learning Torah everywhere should bring the ingathering of the exiles and the great nechamah.

catalogTitle: חיזוק: גודל אהבת ה' אלינו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael has levels that can never be cut off, so that even after the breaking of the luchos brought forgetting, Hashem does not forget Sinai and cannot exchange the Jewish people.

abstract.en: After brief introductions, the Rav ties Elul's 'Ani l'dodi' to the seven haftaros of consolation: after six weeks of silence, Klal Yisrael answers on the seventh with 'Sos asis' as a bride. He turns to 'Vatomer Tziyon azavani Hashem' and the Gemara in Berachos: the golden calf will be forgotten, but Hashem will not forget Sinai. Since the breaking of the luchos brought forgetting into the world, he asks how one can be forgotten and not the other. Bringing the Maharal on the luchos as the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the Midrash in which the king calls his daughter 'my daughter', 'my sister' and 'my mother', he explains that higher levels of love act as a backup that cannot be severed. A Gemara about an esrog of terumah and Rashi in Nitzavim show that Jews are Hashem's terumah and cannot be exchanged. He closes with Yom Kippur, Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah, and the purpose of the yeshiva.

en: In the seventh week of consolation Klal Yisrael finally accepts the consolation and answers Hashem as a bride, with 'Sos asis'.
The Gemara in Berachos teaches that the golden calf will be forgotten but Hashem will not forget Sinai, which seems to contradict itself: either there is forgetting or there is not.
The breaking of the luchos brought forgetting into the world, and threatened to make even the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael forgotten.
Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael has three levels, like a king who calls his daughter 'my daughter', 'my sister' and 'my mother', and the higher levels serve as a backup that cannot be severed.
Klal Yisrael is Hashem's terumah, 'the first of His crop', and just as terumah has no redemption, Hashem cannot exchange the Jewish people for another nation.
Simchas Torah ends the Torah with 'l'einei kol Yisrael', the breaking of the luchos, and at once begins Bereishis, to show that Klal Yisrael is not forgotten.

summary.en: Other speakers thank the yeshiva's supporters and introduce the Rav, mostly in English. The Rav then greets the audience and asks permission to speak sitting.

title.en: Elul and the seventh consolation

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'Ani l'dodi v'dodi li' grows stronger as Rosh Hashanah nears, and that in the seventh haftarah of consolation Klal Yisrael finally answers Hashem as a bride. He recalls the piyut 'Anu ra'yasecha v'atah dodenu' and adds its next line, 'Anu vanecha v'atah avinu', then brings 'Vatomer Tziyon' and 'Hatishkach isha ulah'.

title.en: The broken luchos and forgetting

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos that the golden calf will be forgotten but Sinai will not, and the teaching that the breaking of the luchos brought forgetting. With the Maharal and the Midrash on the luchos' six handbreadths he shows that the luchos were the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and asks why, if forgetting prevailed for the calf, it did not prevail for Sinai.

title.en: Daughter, sister, mother: a bond that holds

summary.en: The Rav answers from the start of the passuk and the Midrash on 'ba'atarah she'itrah lo imo': a king calls his beloved daughter 'my sister', 'my daughter' and finally 'my mother'. A wife's bond can be severed, a daughter's cannot but can know anger, and a mother's love for her infant knows none. With the parable of a hospital's backup generator he explains that when the calf cut the bond of bride and groom, the higher levels remained.

title.en: Klal Yisrael is terumah

summary.en: The Rav brings a Gemara about an esrog of terumah, where the Amora declares sharply that terumah has no redemption, and asks why he speaks with such zeal. He answers with the Midrash of the king who sends away his queen and orders her a necklace, with 'Kodesh Yisrael laShem reishis tevuasoh' and with Rashi in Nitzavim: Jews are terumah and cannot be exchanged, and the claim that they were exchanged is Bilaam's.

title.en: Rotzeh ani, Yom Kippur and Simchas Torah

summary.en: Bringing the Rambam, the Rav explains that a Jew's heart is never with the sin, and that Yom Kippur, equal in gematria to 'rotzeh ani', expresses each Jew's will. He traces the rising levels from the last haftarah through Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur to Shemini Atzeres, whose guest is Shlomo HaMelech, and explains why Simchas Torah ends with the breaking of the luchos and at once begins Bereishis.

title.en: The yeshiva's purpose and blessings

summary.en: The Rav sums up the rising levels of the coming days and says the gathering is to show that Jews do not forget Matan Torah, through yeshivos, Torah and mitzvos. He thanks those who came and supported the yeshiva and blesses them with a good year; another speaker then announces a presentation.

catalogTitle: The Marriage of כלל ישראל to Hashem and the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the count of the Jews before Shavuos is the adorning of the kallah, Klal Yisrael, whose 600,000 souls are the 600,000 letters of the Torah, each with his own name and shlichus.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a question: why did the census of Bamidbar need Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im, when a modern census uses whoever has nothing else to do? He then builds the picture of Shavuos as a wedding: Pesach is erusin, Shavuos nisuin; Hashem is the chassan and Klal Yisrael the kallah, and in a second phase Klal Yisrael is the chassan and the Torah the kallah. The 24 ornaments of a kallah are the 24 sefarim of Tanach, read on Shavuos night. The 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah, which can only be counted by knowing what each letter holds, as the aleph holds the Shem Havaya. The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf, when the kallah is counted. Counting 'by names' means each Jew has his own shlichus, which only great tzaddikim can see. He ends with how to keep Shavuos itself: not to sleep through the davening, which is the chuppah.

en: Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and also of Klal Yisrael and the Torah; Pesach is the erusin and Shavuos the nisuin.
The 24 ornaments of the kallah are the 24 sefarim of Tanach, which is why Tanach is said on Shavuos night in the Tikkun Leil Shavuos.
The 600,000 Jews correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah, and each letter is made of further letters, so counting them takes a special knowledge.
'By the number of names' means a collective made of individuals: each Jew has his own name, which is his own shlichus in the world.
The chuppah of Shavuos is the davening, especially the Kedushah of Musaf, so staying up at night and sleeping through the davening misses the purpose.

title.en: The census question and Shavuos as a wedding

summary.en: The Rav asks why counting the Jews needed Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im, when the United States census hires people who have nothing else to do. He then describes Shavuos as a wedding, Pesach as erusin and Shavuos as nisuin, with Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and then Klal Yisrael and the Torah, as chassan and kallah, and explains the Tikkun Leil Shavuos as preparing the kallah's 24 ornaments.

title.en: The kallah's ornaments and the Name of Adnus

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem as He dwells on Klal Yisrael, the kallah, is the Name of Adnus, while the Shem Havaya is beyond us; amen joins the two (26 and 65 make 91). He brings the Midrash that Hashem adorned Chava with 24 ornaments and the teaching that a talmid chacham must know the 24 sefarim, and notes that in the Tikkun Leil Shavuos each sefer is followed by one of the 24 arrangements of the Name of Adnus.

title.en: 600,000 Jews and 600,000 letters

summary.en: Recalling last week's shiur, the Rav says the 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah. He brings the Gemara in Kiddushin that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters, and asks why a plain count finds far fewer; the answer is that each letter contains other letters, as the aleph is made of two yuds and a vav, the gematria of the Shem Havaya.

title.en: Tzelem Elokim on the human face

summary.en: The Rav explains tzelem Elokim as the human structure of 248 limbs matching the 248 positive mitzvos. On a Jew's face one sees the Shem Havaya as before the sin: the two eyes are the two yuds and the nose the vav, and the mouth beneath is a patach, chochmah, as in 'piha paschah bechochmah'; a sin takes this away.

title.en: Aliyos, Atzeres and the aufruf

summary.en: The Rav says that counted properly there are 600,000 letters, and an aliyah is being called to the letters of the Sefer Torah. Shavuos and Shemini Atzeres are both called Atzeres and are both times of contact with the Torah. The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf, when the Jews, the letters, are counted and the kallah is adorned.

title.en: The kallah's eyes and counting by names

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a kallah whose eyes are beautiful needs no further checking, and explains the eyes as the Sanhedrin and nesi'im, so before the count Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im are shown. He then explains 'bemispar shemos': mispar is a collective, shemos is individuality, and from Rashi in Vayishlach a person's name is his shlichus; people are not counted like a farmer's sheep.

title.en: Each Jew's own shlichus, and who can count

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Nazis' numbering of Jews, meant to strip them of individuality, with Hashem's count: each Jew is a letter of the Torah with a shlichus no one else has, like the stars that Hashem calls each by name. Counting Jews this way takes great tzaddikim; he brings the Ramban that coming before Moshe to be counted brought a person merit, and explains the kvitel and the tzaddik who sees a person's purpose and earlier gilgulim, which answers the opening question.

title.en: Why Shevet Levi was not counted

summary.en: The Rav places Shevet Levi in the middle of the camps, corresponding to Vayikra, the middle sefer, and asks how this fits with Levi not being counted. He explains that the extra soul of the bechor was given to the Levi'im, and that Levi is the root of Klal Yisrael, the 22 letters, which in completeness become 22,000; this reconciles the Gemara's 600,000 malachim at Matan Torah with the Midrash's 22,000.

title.en: Rabbeinu Bechaye: the degalim and the malachim

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbeinu Bechaye, who shows that the four degalim correspond to the malachim of the Merkavah that Yechezkel saw, the four chief malachim Michael, Gavriel, Rephael and Uriel. Each degel has three shevatim, and the name of the middle nasi ends with 'el' like the name of a malach; the camp of Israel below is aimed at the camp of the malachim above.

title.en: Shavuos night and the chuppah at Musaf

summary.en: The Rav sums up: the Shabbos before Shavuos the kallah is counted and her beauty shown; on Shavuos night each sefer of Tanach completed forges another golden ornament. Each year there is a new Torah, and when it is read on Shavuos a person should feel he is receiving the whole year's Torah; the chuppah itself is at Musaf, especially the Kedushah of Keser.

title.en: Not sleeping through the chuppah

summary.en: The Rav warns against staying up all night and then sleeping through the holy Shavuos davening, tells of a Rebbe whose Ahavah Rabbah took two hours, and recommends that weaker people sleep three or four hours and then daven properly. He compares it to a chassan who skips the ring, and ends with the exchange at Sinai, when the upper worlds came down and Moshe went up, so on Shavuos one walks in Shamayim.

catalogTitle: נשים: מיר דארפן זיך האלטן שטארק אין די אמעריקאנע בית לבן

oneLiner.en: From Eliezer, who needed Avraham's oath to stay upright in Lavan's house, the Rav teaches that today the whole world, and America above all, is Lavan's house, and that Jewish families must hold strong in tznius and keep growing.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Avraham had to make Eliezer, his great and devoted disciple, swear an oath. He explains the power of an oath: shevuah is related to sheva, seven, and binds a person's seven middos to Hashem's Name, and mashbia shares a root with mashpia, an infusion of strength from Heaven. A story of the Vizhnitzer Rebbe shows that every soul swears before birth to be a tzaddik. Lavan's house was the headquarters of the Satan, and Eliezer, who had a personal interest, needed the oath to stay upright there. Today, the Rav says, the world and especially America is Lavan's house, and he lists ways to hold strong. He brings the Divrei Yechezkel on the clothes Eliezer gave Rivka and the clothes Hashem made for Adam and Chava. He closes with Chanukah's lesson of constant growth, a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer, and hachnasas kallah.

en: Avraham made even Eliezer, a great talmid chacham and devoted disciple, swear before sending him to find a match for Yitzchak.
An oath binds a person's seven middos to Hashem's Name and draws strength from Heaven to do His will.
Lavan's house was the headquarters of the Satan, and to stay upright there even Eliezer needed the kedushah of the oath.
Today the whole world, and especially America, is Lavan's house, and it is very hard to keep tznius and kedushah in it.
Like the Chanukah lights that keep increasing, a Jew and a Jewish couple must always keep growing better.

candidateTopics: holding strong against the yetzer hara

title.en: Why Eliezer had to swear

summary.en: The Rav opens with the parsha: Avraham sends Eliezer to find a wife for Yitzchak and first makes him swear. He describes Eliezer as a great talmid chacham who taught Avraham's Torah and risked his life for his rebbe, and asks why such a person needed an oath.

title.en: The power of an oath

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a soul is made to swear before birth to be a tzaddik, and explains that shevuah comes from sheva, the seven middos, and that mashbia is related to mashpia. He tells how the Vizhnitzer Rebbe wept on Rosh Hashanah night at the words 'lo nishba l'mirmah' and explained it as the soul's oath.

title.en: Lavan's house, headquarters of the Satan

summary.en: Citing the Zera Kodesh, the Rav describes the house of Besuel and Lavan as the headquarters of the sitra achra, where the tumah was so strong that one had to thank Hashem for not sinning. Since Eliezer had a personal interest, wanting his own daughter for Yitzchak, he needed the holy influence of Avraham's oath to stay upright there.

title.en: America today is Lavan's house

summary.en: The Rav says that before Moshiach a great tumah comes into the world, and today the whole world, especially America, is Lavan's house. He contrasts this with America of seventy years ago, showing the old public school buildings in Williamsburg with separate doors for boys and girls, and praises families who still live with tznius and kedushah, the Eliezers of today.

title.en: How to hold strong in Lavan's house

summary.en: The Rav lists what keeps a Jew strong: attachment to tzaddikim, a rav for every family's questions, gatherings for chizuk, mussar seforim and erliche friends. He speaks of the endless new 'keilim' of the yetzer hara, and of last week's storm, bringing Rashi that immorality brings destruction that strikes good and bad alike, and the Gemara that tzaddikim suffer first. He ends with the struggle of Jewish daughters against today's styles.

title.en: Clothes for Rivka and for Adam and Chava

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Yechezkel's question how Eliezer knew Rivka's size when he brought her clothes, and his answer that he brought a sample of the clothing worn in Avraham's house. He then asks why Hashem made garments for Adam and Chava when they had already made coverings, and explains that Hashem showed what clothing He is pleased with.

title.en: Chanukah's growth and hachnasas kallah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah's 'mosif v'holech' teaches constant growth, and brings a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer that a wife cannot object that her husband became more stringent. He praises the tznius of the women's section of the beis medrash, says a woman dressed less modestly should not be rebuked but helped with grace, and closes with hachnasas kallah and a brachah.

catalogTitle: אמונה - יסוד של כל המצוות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why emunah, the first mitzvah of the heart, is not just one mitzvah among the 613 but the foundation on which all of them stand.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the order of the Sefer Chareidim, which arranges the mitzvos by the limbs of the body and begins with the heart; its first mitzvah is emunah, from the verse 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha'. The 613 mitzvos build the body with which a person will rise at techiyas hameisim, so one who lacks emunah, a mitzvah of the heart, cannot rise at all. Yaakov's request for bread and a garment hints at Torah as the soul's food and mitzvos as its garments in the next world. He discusses gilgul and how learning about a mitzvah one cannot keep counts for it. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on emunah, then the dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613: the Ramban compares it to a building's basement. Every mitzvah is a command, but 'Anochi' is a statement, and it names the exodus from Egypt, which the whole people saw.

en: The Sefer Chareidim orders the mitzvos by the limbs, beginning with the heart, and the first mitzvah of the heart is emunah.
Each limb is built for techiyas hameisim by the mitzvah connected to it, and without emunah, a mitzvah of the heart, a person cannot rise at all.
Torah is the soul's food in Gan Eden and the mitzvos are its garments.
The Rishonim dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613; the Ramban holds it is not, because it is their foundation, like the basement of a building.
Every mitzvah, even those of the heart, is given as a command, but 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha' is worded as a statement.
Jewish emunah is based on the exodus from Egypt, where the whole people saw that Hashem controls nature.

mitzvos and the limbs of the body
Torah as food and mitzvos as garments
exodus from Egypt as basis of emunah

title.en: Sefer Chareidim: the heart and the first mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Sefer Chareidim orders the mitzvos by the limbs, starting with the heart, whose first mitzvah is emunah. He explains that the 613 mitzvos build the body for techiyas hameisim, so a person without emunah cannot rise, and mentions the garment made of the mitzvos.

title.en: Bread and garment: Torah and mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov, in danger, asked only for bread and a garment, and answers that in the next world Torah is the soul's food and mitzvos its garments. He discusses gilgul for a mitzvah not yet kept, the mitzvos that cannot be kept in galus, and how learning about a mitzvah counts for it.

title.en: Why learn emunah; Chavakuk's one mitzvah

summary.en: Returning to emunah, the Rav says that without it a Jew has no connection to the World to Come, and explains why the shiurim came to focus on this one mitzvah. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh', and explains it means concentrating on one mitzvah through which all are kept.

title.en: Is emunah one of the 613? The basement

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Gemara does not list the 613, so the Rishonim counted them and disagree on some, emunah among them. The Rambam counts it; the Ramban does not, because it is the foundation of the mitzvos, like a basement that is not counted as a room yet holds the whole building. He adds that every mitzvah in the Torah is worded as a command.

title.en: A command to love; 'Anochi' and the exodus

summary.en: The Rav explains that even love and fear of Hashem are commanded, since every Jew already loves Hashem and must only reveal it, whereas 'Anochi' is a statement, not a command. He asks why it mentions the exodus rather than creation, and answers that our emunah rests on the exodus, which the whole people saw; the end of the recording is badly garbled.

catalogTitle: Side 1: Every Jew is an אות & a מצוה Side 2: מתן תורה - The Foundation of Emunah

oneLiner.en: The Rav presents Shavuos as a Yovel of return, when every Jew goes back to his own letter and mitzvah in the Torah, and shows that Matan Torah, witnessed by an entire nation, is the foundation of emunah that is relived every year.

abstract.en: In the first talk the Rav approaches Shavuos through the law of Yovel, return. The Eved Ivri who was uprooted from the family of Klal Yisrael goes back at Yovel to his family and his portion in Eretz Yisrael; so too every Jew is one of the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah and is rooted in one of the 613 mitzvos, and Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a small Yovel when he returns to his letter and his mitzvah. He shows this law of return in nature, in the ger, and in Rus and Yisro, calls for heartfelt prayer for Torah, and tells how the Sanzer Rav's son saw Matan Torah anew. In the second talk he reads the pesukim of Va'eschanan and Yisro: an entire nation heard Hashem speak, which no other religion can claim, and this was passed down without a break, so a Jew knows Matan Torah rather than merely believes it. It repeats every Shavuos, and he urges davening and hearing the Torah reading with full kavanah.

en: Shavuos, the fiftieth day after seven weeks of Sefirah, is a miniature Yovel: a day of returning to one's roots.
Every Jew is one letter of the Sefer Torah, corresponding to the 600,000 souls, and belongs exactly in his place in it.
Every Jew is rooted in one particular mitzvah, and the mitzvah of this generation before Mashiach is emunah.
Matan Torah was witnessed by an entire nation who all became prophets, unlike other religions built on one individual's claim.
A tradition witnessed by millions and passed from father to son is irrefutable, so a Jew knows Matan Torah rather than only believing it.
Matan Torah repeats itself every Shavuos, and each Jew receives his portion in Torah for the coming year.

every Jew as a letter in the Sefer Torah
emunah in the generation before Mashiach
Ahavah Rabbah and tefillah for Torah

title.en: One road to Shavuos: seven weeks to the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Rav says the Torah, and so Shavuos, is infinite, and he will approach it from one of many roads. He describes the seven weeks of Sefirah leading to the fiftieth day and introduces Yovel, which means return.

title.en: The Eved Ivri returns to his family

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Eved Ivri, permitted to a shifcha, is uprooted from the family of Klal Yisrael; shifcha is mishpacha without the mem. At Yovel he is dragged back to his family and his nachalah, and the Ramban explains Yovel as going back to the roots.

title.en: Shavuos as a miniature Yovel

summary.en: Every Jew has a letter in the Sefer Torah, and one who does not keep it uproots himself. The Rav links the shofar of freedom, the great shofar at Sinai and the shofar of Yovel, calls Shavuos a miniature Yovel, and notes that Parshas Behar on Shemitah and Yovel is read before Shavuos.

title.en: Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: From the counting in Bamidbar, the lots of Eretz Yisrael and the four camps around the Mishkan corresponding to the five Chumashim, the Rav shows that each Jew has his exact place. The ben ha-Mitzri was an extra letter; at hagbahah one tries to see his own letter, and the Shabbos before Shavuos returns each Jew to it.

title.en: Every Jew's own mitzvah; ours is emunah

summary.en: Each Jew is rooted in one of the 613 mitzvos, as Reb Naftali of Ropshitz was bound to the mitzvah of sukkah, and each generation has its mitzvah; the Rav says ours is emunah, which explains today's heresy. The 620 letters of the Aseres Hadibros are the 613 mitzvos plus the seven rabbinic ones, and on Shavuos each Jew binds himself to his letter.

title.en: The law of return: nature, the ger, Rus and Yisro

summary.en: The Rav shows a universal law that everything returns to its source: a thrown stone, water and rivers, as in Koheles, and the neshamah. A ger has a Jewish soul that finds no rest until it returns; therefore on Shavuos we read of Rus who 'returned' and of Yisro, whose names share their letters.

title.en: Praying for Torah; the Sanzer Rav's son sees Matan Torah

summary.en: The Rav says Shavuos is a special time to pray for Torah, recalling tzaddikim whose Ahavah Rabbah lasted hours in tears. Each Shavuos Matan Torah is given again and each Jew gets his portion for the year, a Rosh Hashanah for Torah. He tells how the Sanzer Rav's son, who went to Belz for Shavuos, saw the thunder and lightning of Matan Torah at his father's.

title.en: A people of mesiras nefesh returns to the Torah

summary.en: The Rav says Shavuos is not a commemoration but a reliving of Matan Torah. Jews come from a stock that gave their lives rather than abandon Torah; each should accept the Torah despite hardship, return to his roots and bring others closer. He closes with Shavuos as the day of David HaMelech and a wish for the great Yovel.

title.en: Second talk: Hashem speaks through the Chumash

summary.en: Opening a second talk, the Rav says he will not offer his own derashah: in the Chumash Hashem Himself speaks to us. He asks listeners not to learn Chumash as in cheder but to listen attentively to every word.

title.en: What your eyes saw: a nation of prophets

summary.en: The Rav reads 'rak hishamer lecha' in Va'eschanan: do not forget what your eyes saw at Chorev. Other religions rest on one charismatic man's claim; at Sinai every Jew became a prophet and heard Hashem face to face, and the pasuk commands passing this to children and grandchildren.

title.en: An irrefutable chain of tradition

summary.en: The Rav compares Matan Torah to historical facts no one doubts, since a lie witnessed by multitudes cannot pass down the generations. The Torah was written within forty years while witnesses lived, every Jewish community has the same Sefer Torah, and each generation is a link in the chain.

title.en: The third day at Sinai repeats every year

summary.en: Turning to Parshas Yisro, the Rav reads 'atem re'isem': at the Exodus they saw but were not prophets, while at Sinai they would be. He describes the thunder, lightning and trembling of the third day, and explains that every Yom Tov's event repeats; shanah means repetition, and on Shavuos each Jew receives his Torah for the year.

title.en: Hidden by the body; knowing, not believing

summary.en: Hashem speaks to every Jew on Shavuos, but the body and aveiros insulate us; great tzaddikim showed their talmidim the thunder and lightning. The Rav reads 'ki she'al na': no nation ever heard G-d speak from the fire, and 'atah hor'esa lada'as', as Rav Hirsch stresses, means we know Matan Torah rather than believe it.

title.en: The avodah of Shavuos: hearing and visualizing

summary.en: The Rav says each Yom Tov has its activity, and Shavuos's is hearing the word of Hashem. One should say Ahavah Rabbah with great feeling, visualize standing at Sinai when the Aseres Hadibros are read, and remember Matan Torah, one of the six zechiros. He warns not to stay up all night and then sleep through davening.

title.en: The groom without a ring; a prayer for the shofar of Mashiach

summary.en: With a parable of a groom who pays for everything but the ring, the Rav says the main thing is davening and the Torah reading. He speaks of Klal Yisrael's need for salvation, and closes with the Midrash of Yitzchak's ram: its left horn sounded at Matan Torah and its right horn will be the shofar of Mashiach.

catalogTitle: אמונה - ירושה מאבותינו הקדושים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, an inborn trait like an animal's instinct, so the mitzvah is not to acquire it but not to spoil it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the dispute between the Rambam and the Ramban whether emunah is counted among the 613 mitzvos, and asks why the mitzvah of 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement and not as a command. To explain, he distinguishes acquired traits, such as knowledge and good habits, from hereditary ones, such as height and eye color, and shows from the instincts of spiders, beavers, birds and bees that even knowledge can be inherited. Emunah is such an inheritance: Jews are believers, sons of believers. A Jew who seems not to believe has a sick emunah, made ill mainly by forbidden foods and arayos, and must go to a tzaddik for a cure. Following Rav Tzadok HaKohen, the mitzvah is not to spoil this fact. He urges learning Chumash with Rashi and Ramban, and closes with the spark of Avraham in every Jew, guarded by Hashem as 'Magen Avraham'.

en: Some traits are acquired from outside, like knowledge and trained habits, while others pass by inheritance, like hair and eye color.
Animal instincts, like the spider's web and the bird's migration, show that even knowledge can be inherited.
A Jew's emunah in Hashem is an inheritance; Jews are 'believers, sons of believers'.
A Jew whose emunah is weak has made it sick, mainly through forbidden foods and arayos, and needs a tzaddik to heal him.
The mitzvah of emunah is written as a fact because Jews are born with it; the command is not to spoil it.
Every Jew carries a piece of Avraham Avinu within him, a spark that can never be extinguished.

candidateTopics: mitzvah of emunah in the Rambam
sin as a sickness of the soul
forbidden foods and dulling of the heart
learning Chumash with Rashi and Ramban

title.en: Is emunah a mitzvah? Acquired and inherited traits

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Rambam-Ramban dispute whether emunah is counted among the 613 mitzvos, and asks why 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement rather than a command. He begins his answer by distinguishing traits acquired from outside, like knowledge and trained habits, from hereditary ones, like height, eye color and hair color.

title.en: Inherited knowledge: instinct and emunah

summary.en: Knowledge itself normally comes from outside, but the Rav shows from the spider's web, the beaver's dam, birds' migration and the bees' honeycomb that some knowledge is inherited. So it is no wonder that a Jew's emunah comes by inheritance, and Jews who do not believe have made their emunah sick.

title.en: Believers, sons of believers; healing a sick emunah

summary.en: From Moshe Rabbeinu's words 'they will not believe me' and Hashem's reply that they are believers, sons of believers, the Rav shows that emunah, love and fear of Hashem are inherited from Avraham and Yitzchak. Where they are weak, the soul is sick, and as the Rambam says, it must be healed like the body: a man who ruined his appetite still has it and needs a doctor to restore it.

title.en: What sickens emunah, and the mitzvah not to spoil it

summary.en: Every sin weakens emunah, but especially questionable food and arayos, which clog the soul like cholesterol clogs the heart; the cure is to go to the tzaddik for a prescription of learning, davening and tzedakah. The Rav then answers his opening question, developing Rav Tzadok HaKohen: the mitzvah is written as a fact because a Jew is born believing, and the command is not to spoil that fact.

title.en: The parshiyos of the Avos as the foundation of emunah

summary.en: Turning to the parshiyos about to be learned, beginning with Avraham's birth at the end of Noach, the Rav says the stories of the Avos and Yetzias Mitzrayim are the foundation of emunah, and brings the Chasam Sofer that a Jew must regularly learn Chumash with Rashi and Ramban. Once emunah was absorbed at home and in the shtetl; today, when many shuls are social institutions, it must be drawn from the seforim.

title.en: The spark of Avraham in every Jew

summary.en: Emunah is inherited from Avraham Avinu, the first to truly believe, and the first mention of emunah in the Torah is his. With the parable of a tree containing all the trees that grow from its seeds, the Rav explains that every Jew was once part of Avraham and carries a piece of him, a spark or pilot light that no waters can extinguish. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that in 'Magen Avraham' we thank Hashem for guarding this point.

catalogTitle: טעם של כפירה הוא rationalization

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that kefirah is not a conclusion of the mind but a rationalization of the heart: a person who does not want to carry the Torah's demands fools himself with denial and invented reasons.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the teaching of tzaddikim that fooling oneself is worse than fooling others, since the one who deceives others at least knows the truth. Chazal read 'do not stray after your hearts' as minus, heresy: kefirah comes from the heart, the seat of desires, not from the mind. Psychology, a new science, names two forms of this self-deception. Denial: Chiel of Beis El kept building Yericho while his sons died one by one under Yehoshua's curse; the ostrich hides its head in the sand; the smoker insists cigarettes will not harm him. Rationalization: the ba'al gaavah invents reasons to defend his pride, the bochur blames everything but himself, the wolf calls the grapes sour. This, the Rav says, is the secret of the apikores: Hashem is visible everywhere, but the Torah is too hard for them, so they build ever-changing theories of creation. Every Jew truly believes; old people return to teshuvah once their desires fade, while those driven by gaavah often do not.

en: Following the tzaddikim, the Rav says one must guard even more against fooling oneself than against fooling others, because self-deception hides the truth even from the deceiver.
Chazal read 'after your hearts' as heresy: kefirah comes from the heart, the source of desires, and a person can fool himself because he has desires.
Denial means refusing to admit what a person knows deep down, as with Chiel of Beis El, the ostrich and the smoker.
Rationalization means inventing reasons to protect one's pride or desire, like the wolf who declared the grapes he could not reach to be sour.
The apikores denies creation not because the Torah's account makes no sense, but because the Torah's demands are too hard for him, so he builds his own theories.
Every Jew believes in the Ribono shel Olam even when he calls himself an apikores; he only denies it, and even a non-Jew can see Hashem through His deeds.

title.en: Fooling oneself and the heart's desires

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Torah's ban on lying to others with the tzaddikim's warning against fooling oneself, and brings Chazal that 'after your hearts' means heresy, which grows from desires. He notes that psychology, a new science, sheds light on this, adding the Chazon Ish's reply that Chumash and Rashi already teach it.

title.en: Denial: Chiel, the ostrich and the smoker

summary.en: The Rav tells how Chiel of Beis El rebuilt Yericho despite Yehoshua's curse, losing his sons one by one, and asks why he did not stop. The answer is denial, which he illustrates with the bird that buries its head in the sand and the smoker who insists his cigarette will not harm him.

title.en: Rationalization and the sour grapes

summary.en: The Rav defines rationalization as inventing reasons to defend one's pride or desire: the ba'al gaavah who keeps his pride, the bochur who blames his chavrusa, rebbi and the room for not learning, the man who blames the hammer. He tells the fable of the wolf who could not climb the fence and declared the grapes sour.

title.en: Why apikorsim invent theories of creation

summary.en: The Rav asks why apikorsim, who inherited emunah and can see Hashem in nature, history and events, invent ever-changing theories of creation instead of accepting the Chumash. He recalls the evolution taught in his school days, and a frum chief physicist who refuted evolution from science to the yeshiva bochurim, and concludes that they deny because the Torah is too hard for them: the sour grapes again.

title.en: No true atheist: teshuvah, taivah and gaavah

summary.en: The Rav argues that no apikores is truly certain; at most he has a doubt, which no one would gamble on, as with poisoned bottles. Old people do teshuvah once their desires fade, while those driven by gaavah often do not. He concludes that every Jew believes and even a non-Jew can see Hashem through His deeds, citing Reb Elchonon Wasserman that a kofer is liable because kefirah is rationalization.

catalogTitle: מאברהם אבינו התחיל אומה שמאמין בה'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Avraham and Sarah had to be barren so that with Avraham a new kind of being would begin, one that believes in Hashem by instinct, and that this emunah passes to every Jew as an inheritance through the mother.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that every Jew inherits his emunah from the Avos, so a denier is not a true heretic but is deceiving himself. He then asks why Avraham and Sarah had to be barren, since nothing in the world is chance; even the word 'mikreh' belongs to the language of impurity. Following the seforim, he explains that barrenness cut Avraham off from the chain of generations: a new creation began with him, a species that believes in Hashem as knowledge in the blood, not only in the mind. This is why Avraham was exempted from honoring his father, and why the world's creation was completed only with Avraham. A kofer, like the pitch on Noach's ark, merely covers over a belief that fills his whole body. Through the three matzos and four cups he shows that intellect comes from the father and feeling from the mother, so emunah, which is feeling, comes from the mother, as the word itself shows, and Jewishness follows the mother. Denial is rationalization, like Eisav blaming his wife.

en: Every Jew inherits emunah from the Avos; one who denies Hashem believes deep inside and is only trying to excuse himself.
Nothing in the world is chance, down to a cup of coffee or a straw moved by the wind; all is hashgacha pratis.
Avraham and Sarah had to be barren to cut them off from the previous generations, so that a new kind of being, one that believes in Hashem by instinct, could begin with them.
Emunah is not a matter of intellect but is part of the Jew's whole body, so a kofer only covers it over.
Intellect comes from the father and feeling from the mother; emunah, being feeling, comes from the mother, which is why a child's Jewishness follows the mother.
Denying Hashem is rationalization, as Eisav blamed his wife for losing the brachos instead of himself.

title.en: Inherited emunah and the barren Avos

summary.en: The Rav recalls that every Jew inherits emunah from the Avos and a denier only fools himself. He asks why Avraham and Sarah had to be barren, stressing that nothing is chance and that the word 'mikreh' is a language of impurity.

title.en: A new species begins with Avraham

summary.en: Bringing the Yismach Moshe, the Rav explains that barrenness cut Avraham and Sarah off from the continuity of the generations, so that a new creation began with Avraham: a species that believes in Hashem by instinct.

title.en: Freed from honoring Terach; creation ends with Avraham

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Torah records Terach's death before Avraham leaves Charan, through the Midrash that Avraham was exempted from honoring his father, since he was a new species. From the pesukim said in the morning davening he shows that creation was completed with Avraham, whose heart was found faithful.

title.en: The kofer only covers over his belief

summary.en: The Rav explains the word 'kofer' from the pitch that covered Noach's ark and from the kofer hakol of the Gemara, who knows he owes the money: a denier only paints over his belief. Emunah, he says, is not in the brain but in the whole body.

title.en: Matzos and cups: emunah comes from the mother

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Seder has three matzos and four cups, and explains that grain gives intellect and corresponds to the Avos, while wine gives feeling and corresponds to the Imahos. Since emunah is feeling, it comes from the mother, which is why Jewishness follows the mother while shevet follows the father.

title.en: Emunah from 'em'; denial as rationalization

summary.en: From the rule that a noun drops the final nun of its verb (shen, gan), the Rav shows that emunah is tied to 'em', mother. He concludes that every Jew believes, and that denial is rationalization, like Eisav blaming his wife for losing the brachos.

catalogTitle: The קדושה of שיר השירים as the Theme of שבועות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, the moment the holiness of Shir HaShirim came down to the world, and that the seven weeks of Sefirah are the kallah's preparation through purifying the seven middos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with this week's mitzvah of rebuke and explains, with the example of an inoculation, why anger shows the rebuke has worked. Turning to Sefirah, he shows that the tenth of the ten utterances of creation is the creation of chassan and kallah, the culmination of the world. Shlomo HaMelech, whose wisdom could only be conveyed through layers of parables, wrote Shir HaShirim as the parable of the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. Shabbos is the kallah, and the tenth and highest holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, corresponds to that union, which is why Shir HaShirim is the holy of holies of Tanach. At Matan Torah this holiness came down into the physical world, so Shavuos is the wedding and the Luchos are the kiddushin. The seven weeks of Sefirah are the kallah's days of purification: refining chesed, gevurah, tiferes, netzach and hod, each embodied by a tzaddik. He closes with the Rambam's laws of holiness and purity in the Sefirah sedros and a story of the Bluzhever Rebbe whose heart raced before Shavuos.

en: When the one being rebuked becomes angry, it shows the rebuke has stirred him, like the reaction that shows an inoculation is working, so the mitzvah has been fulfilled.
The tenth utterance of creation is the creation of chassan and kallah, the culmination of the world, which is why the wedding blessing uses the word 'bara'.
Shir HaShirim is Shlomo HaMelech's parable for the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, which the human mind cannot grasp directly.
The tenth and highest holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, corresponds to the tenth utterance, the union of chassan and kallah, and Shir HaShirim is the Kodesh HaKodashim of Tanach.
Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem with Knesses Yisrael; the Luchos are the kiddushin, and therefore they rest in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
The seven weeks of Sefirah are like the kallah's seven days of purity, given to purify the seven middos before coming to the chuppah.

Shir HaShirim as holy of holies

title.en: Rebuke and the sign that it worked

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's dispute on how far one must rebuke, asks how it knows rebuke continues until the other gets angry, and answers with an inoculation: the angry reaction shows the rebuke is working and the mitzvah is done.

title.en: The tenth utterance: chassan and kallah

summary.en: Turning to Sefirah as preparation for Matan Torah, the Rav discusses the ten utterances of creation and shows that the tenth, the creation of chassan and kallah, is the culmination of creation; he then introduces Shlomo HaMelech and his parables.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand parables

summary.en: The Rav asks what is special about Shlomo's parables, and explains in the name of the Ba'al HaTanya that his thought was so deep that he had to lower it through three thousand parables, each explaining the one above, before people began to grasp it.

title.en: Shir HaShirim and the menuchah of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav introduces Shir HaShirim as speaking of chassan and kallah, tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov and a boy singing it with fervor, and explains from Rashi that what was created on Shabbos is menuchah, the settledness of a married woman.

title.en: Shir HaShirim as the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shir HaShirim is the parable for the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, that Shabbos is the kallah, and that the tenth of the ten holinesses, the Kodesh HaKodashim with its keruvim, corresponds to that union; therefore Rabbi Akiva calls Shir HaShirim holy of holies.

title.en: Matan Torah as the wedding

summary.en: The Rav says that at Matan Torah the holiness of Shir HaShirim came down into the physical world; Matan Torah was like a chuppah, wedding customs mirror it, Shavuos is the day of the nesuin, and the Luchos are the kiddushin kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim.

title.en: Sefirah: purifying the middos

summary.en: The Rav compares Sefirah to the kallah's seven days of purity, asks why the Torah says so little about middos, and answers that good middos are the prerequisite for Torah; Sefer Bereishis teaches middos through the Avos, and in these weeks one must purify seven middos.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav explains chesed as love, used for good or for indulgence, with Avraham as its tzaddik; gevurah as holding back, embodied by Yitzchak; and Yishmael as the refuse of Avraham's chesed, like the side effects of a medicine.

title.en: Tiferes, netzach, hod and their blends

summary.en: The Rav describes Esav as the klipah of gevurah and Yaakov as the blend called tiferes, like harmony in color and music; from Pasach Eliyahu he explains netzach and hod as the two legs, standing by fighting or by yielding; and with a mother holding her child he shows gevurah within chesed.

title.en: Kedushah and taharah in the Sefirah sedros

summary.en: The Rav points out that all the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah are found in the sedros read during Sefirah, from Shemini to Kedoshim, because these are days of holiness and purity before the chuppah.

title.en: The Bluzhever Rebbe's racing heart

summary.en: The Rav tells how a doctor found the Bluzhever Rebbe's heart beating abnormally shortly before Shavuos, and the Rebbe answered that he was about to receive the Torah; he closes that Shavuos must not come unprepared, since then the Torah of the whole year is given anew.

catalogTitle: מבשרי אחזה אלוקי

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Hashem cannot be grasped by philosophy, since human intellect is not a sense made for G-dliness, yet a person can recognize that there is a Creator by looking at the wonders of his own body, as in 'from my flesh I see G-d'.

abstract.en: The Rav distinguishes two paths to emunah: the inherited, instinctive faith of Jews as believers descended from believers, and chakirah, philosophical inquiry, the path of the Rambam in his Moreh Nevuchim. He describes the dispute over philosophy, with the sages of Ashkenaz, especially the Rosh, forbidding it, and notes that philosophy is a foreign import found nowhere in Chumash, Shas or Midrash; the Acharonim, the Vilna Gaon among them, distanced themselves from it entirely. Philosophy fails, he explains, because the intellect is no more made to perceive Hashem than the ear is made to see a picture. The faculty for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh, present in every Jew through his neshamah but insulated by aveiros. Still, from the creations one can recognize that there is a Creator: 'from my flesh I see G-d'. He describes the eye, heart, blood vessels, lungs and digestion, an anatomy book, and a watch that could never assemble itself.

en: There are two paths to emunah: the inherited, felt faith of Jews as believers descended from believers, and chakirah, philosophical inquiry, as the Rambam did in Moreh Nevuchim.

Philosophy is a foreign import: no argument proving Hashem's existence by logic is found in Chumash, Shas or Midrash, and the Rishonim of Ashkenaz and later the Acharonim distanced themselves from it.
The intellect cannot grasp Hashem, just as no amount of hearing can hear a picture; the faculty for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh.
Every Jew has ruach hakodesh because of his neshamah, but aveiros insulate the body from the neshamah like insulation on a live wire.
Through the creations, though not in His essence, one can understand that there is a Ribono shel Olam, and a person need only look at his own body: 'from my flesh I see G-d'.

The eye, heart, blood vessels, lungs and digestive system each adjust and repair themselves automatically, and one cannot say they made themselves, just as shaking watch parts will never produce a watch.
