title.en: Two paths to emunah: feeling and inquiry

summary.en: The Rav recalls that Jews are believers descended from believers, holding emunah as an instinctive inheritance from the Avos. He then presents the second path, chakirah, logical inquiry, and describes the Rambam's Moreh Nevuchim as its chief example, approaching Hashem, Torah from Heaven and reward and punishment through reason.

title.en: The dispute over philosophy

summary.en: The Rav describes how Rishonim attacked the Rambam's approach, how the sages of Ashkenaz, especially the Rosh, forbade philosophy and even made a cherem, while the Sefardi sages valued it. He stresses that philosophy is found nowhere in Chumash, Shas or Midrash, that the Acharonim, including the Vilna Gaon, rejected it entirely, and that Hashem cannot be 'figured out' like a mathematical problem.

title.en: Five senses, intellect and ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Rav explains that our five senses connect us to our surroundings but none is made for G-dliness, and the intellect is likewise the wrong faculty, like trying to hear a picture. The sense for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh, present in every Jew through his neshamah; aveiros insulate a person from it like insulation on a live wire.

title.en: From my flesh I see G-d: the eye

summary.en: The Rav says the Acharonim warned against philosophy today, yet through Hashem's creations, though not His essence, one can understand that there is a Creator. Citing Iyov's 'from my flesh I see G-d', he describes the eye in detail: the retina, lens and pupil that adjusts to light, the eyelashes and tears that protect and clean it, its self-healing, and two eyes working together for depth.

title.en: The heart, blood, lungs and digestion

summary.en: The Rav describes the heart, a plain piece of muscle that beats for a lifetime and speeds up and slows down by itself, the fifty thousand miles of blood vessels that carry food and oxygen and remove waste, the lungs that adjust automatically, and the digestive system beginning with the teeth, asking whether all this came about by itself.

title.en: The anatomy book and the watch

summary.en: The Rav adds the sense of taste and saliva, then tells of an anatomy book he found in an apartment in Eretz Yisrael, with wonders on every page such as why the spine is curved. He closes with the parable of a watch whose parts could never assemble themselves in a shaking machine, concluding that even a non-Jew should recognize the Creator simply by looking at his own body.

catalogTitle: הכרה של אמונה ע"י נפלאות הבריאה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows from the wonders and the precise balance of nature, the human body and history that the world cannot have come about by itself, and that people who claim it did are rationalizing so as not to see the Ribono shel Olam.

abstract.en: Continuing from his earlier talk on the wonders of the human body, the Rav widens the view to all of nature: plants and animals depend on each other for oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the planets are held in a balance that a small shift would destroy. He brings the parable of the Chovos HaLevavos about a magnificent picture that someone claimed came from spilled ink, and calls the belief that the world made itself an even greater madness, a rationalization. He illustrates this with a story from Telz: a member of a club of maskilim stopped coming after a halacha about burying a dead man's blood revealed the Ribono shel Olam, because it took away his peace of mind. The Rav then brings more wonders: the fixed 21 percent of oxygen in the air, cells that renew themselves except those of the brain, blood clotting, and water that expands as it freezes so that ice floats. He closes with Hashem's guidance seen in history and in the protection of every small child.

en: All parts of nature depend on each other, like the systems of the body: plants give off oxygen for animals and live from what animals give off, and the planets are held in a delicate balance.
Saying the world came about by itself is a greater madness than saying a masterpiece came from spilled ink; it is a rationalization.
People avoid seeing the Ribono shel Olam because recognizing Him would take away their freedom to do as they please.
The exact makeup of the air, the renewal of cells, blood clotting and the unusual behavior of water as it freezes are all wonders of the Ribono shel Olam that keep life possible.
Just as Hashem is seen in physics, He is seen in history, especially Jewish history, in current events and in the protection of every child.

title.en: The interdependence of all of nature

summary.en: The Rav recalls that he spoke about the wonders of the body, and widens it to nature: animals and plants cannot exist without each other, exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the planets are held in a balance that would collapse if one left its orbit.

title.en: The Chovos HaLevavos's parable of the ink

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chovos HaLevavos's parable of a magnificent picture that someone claimed was made by ink bottles spilled by the wind, and says that believing the world made itself is a greater madness. He calls it a rationalization and begins to recount how, during a war in Eretz Yisroel, even secular newspapers reported the miracles.

title.en: The club house in Telz

summary.en: The Rav tells a story from a sefer about Telz: after a member of a club of maskilim took his own life, plaster kept falling from the ceiling until the Rosh Yeshiva's halacha about burying a dead man's blood was followed. One member then stopped coming, because seeing the Ribono shel Olam took away his peace of mind; the Rav says one need not go to such a club house to see Him.

title.en: Oxygen, cells and blood clotting

summary.en: The Rav explains that the air holds exactly 21 percent oxygen, enough to breathe and not so much that one match would set the world on fire. He then describes how the body's cells die and are replaced within seven years, except the brain cells that hold memory, and how a substance in the blood makes it clot so that a cut does not bleed a person to death.

title.en: Why ice floats

summary.en: The Rav explains that every substance expands with heat and contracts with cold, as in a thermometer, but water near freezing reverses and expands, which is why a frozen bottle bursts. Because of this, ice stays on top of a river as a blanket and the fish below survive; were it otherwise the river would fill with ice from the bottom and all life in it would die.

title.en: Hashem in history and in raising children

summary.en: The Rav asks whether, with millions of such wonders, one can say the world made itself, mentions sleep as another wonder, and says that just as Hashem is seen in physics He is seen in history, especially Jewish history, and in daily events. He ends with the protection Hashem gives every small child through countless dangers, so that the boys before him grew up healthy.

catalogTitle: התבוננות בנפלאות הבריאה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in our time, when open miracles are not seen, the mitzvah is to believe, yet one who contemplates his surroundings can still see wonders, such as the striking number of Kohanim and Levi'im among the great teachers of halachah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that today we see no great revelations or miracles, while our grandparents told reliable stories of tzaddikim. He tells one such story, recorded by the Maharsham's son: the Maharsham, a great masmid as a young man, fell gravely ill; a messenger was sent to Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov, and at that very hour the Maharsham saw his heavenly judgment, where a dark angel blew his Torah off the scale until a young black-bearded dayan defended Torah learned even not purely for Heaven's sake. Later he recognized that dayan as Reb Ayzikl, who told him to always be lenient for Jews. The Rav then explains that today the mitzvah is to believe, and believing is greater than seeing, as the Kotzker Rebbe answered. Still, contemplating our surroundings shows wonders: Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that Levi would teach Torah to Israel is visible in how many Kohanim and Levi'im are among the commentators on Shulchan Aruch, the later poskim, the Brisk line and even the roshei yeshiva in the beis medrash.

en: Today there are no open miracles because the mitzvah of our time is emunah, and believing is greater than seeing.
Not every story of tzaddikim is reliable, since many were embellished or invented, but some were recorded by trustworthy people and can be relied on.
In the Maharsham's story, the Torah he had learned saved him in the heavenly judgment, because even Torah not learned purely for Heaven's sake is precious above in a time of deep exile.
One who contemplates his surroundings can see wonders today as well, which show that there is a Ribono shel Olam.

Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that the tribe of Levi will teach Torah to Israel is fulfilled to this day in the disproportionate number of Kohanim and Levi'im among the great poskim and teachers of Torah.

title.en: Stories of tzaddikim and the Maharsham's diligence

summary.en: The Rav notes that today no great miracles are seen, while our grandparents told reliable stories of tzaddikim. He introduces the Maharsham, a great posek known for leniency, asks where this came from, and describes how the Minchas Chinuch told him at his semichah to learn constantly, even in spare minutes on Shabbos.

title.en: The Maharsham's illness and heavenly judgment

summary.en: The Rav tells how the young Maharsham fell gravely ill, a messenger was sent to Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov, and at the crisis he saw his judgment in Heaven: a dark angel blew his Torah off the scale until a black-bearded young dayan defended Torah learned even not for its own sake. Later he recognized Reb Ayzikl as that dayan and was told to always be lenient for Jews, which the Rav says explains the Maharsham's leniency.

title.en: Believing is greater than seeing

summary.en: The Rav explains that today the mitzvah is to believe, and tells how the Kotzker Rebbe answered a tzaddik who claimed to see the ushpizin with his eyes: he believes they come, and believing is greater than seeing. Yet contemplating our surroundings reveals wonders, and he begins his example: Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing that Levi will teach Torah, and the Chemdas Shlomo's observation that almost all the commentators on Shulchan Aruch are from Levi.

title.en: Kohanim and Levi'im as Israel's teachers

summary.en: The Rav goes through the Shulchan Aruch and its commentators, the later poskim and the Brisk line of roshei yeshiva, showing how many are Kohanim or Levi'im, far beyond their share of the people, and notes that Chassidic Rebbes come from the house of David. He counts the roshei yeshiva sitting at the mizrach wall, finds seven Kohanim and Levi'im against four Yisraelim, and concludes that one sees here the truth of the Torah, three and a half thousand years after Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of מגילת רות: The redemption of רות, the נשמה of יובל, from the bondage of מואב

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Megillas Rus as the megillah of Yovel, the return of a lost soul to its roots: Rus, a neshama of Yovel, is drawn out of Moav to Beis Lechem, and even her descendant Menashe is brought back through Hashem's hidden tunnel of teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shavuos as a day of Yovel, of returning to one's roots, set against the eved who cuts himself off from the Jewish family and refuses the 'rope' of Shabbos until the shofar of Yovel drags him out. Megillas Rus is the megillah of Yovel; just as Yovel exists in time and in the soul, it has a place, Beis Lechem, the home of David and Mashiach. Naomi, wife of Elimelech, goes to Moav to bring back Rus, a neshama of Yovel. Boaz hints to Rus that Menashe will come from her, and the Rav asks why he would tell her such a painful thing. Through the Gemara's story of Rav Ashi and Menashe, he answers that even Menashe teaches Klal Yisrael how to make hamotzi. He explains Hashem's tunnel for Menashe's teshuvah as yibum, the tikkun of souls, ties it to the neshamos in our bread, and closes with preparing for Shavuos.

en: Shavuos is a day of Yovel: a return of every Jew to his roots and to the Jewish family, which the counting of Klal Yisrael by families prepares.
Yovel exists in time, in the soul and in a place; its place is Beis Lechem, home of David HaMelech and Mashiach, who gathers Jews back to Eretz Yisrael.
Boaz's hint that Menashe would descend from Rus was meant as comfort: even Menashe would teach Klal Yisrael the halacha of hamotzi.
Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah through a hidden tunnel because there is a level of Torah higher than the angels can grasp, where every Jew must return.
Yibum is the tikkun of souls, a 'tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod', and it is connected to Mashiach.
Food holds neshamos awaiting their tikkun; eating with washing, a bracha and kavanah elevates them, while careless eating lowers them.

hamotzi and the neshama in bread

title.en: Shavuos, Yovel and the eved who leaves the family

summary.en: The Rav introduces Rus and Boaz and calls Shavuos a day of Yovel, a return to one's roots. He contrasts the eved who cuts himself off from the Jewish family and refuses the 'rope' of Shabbos, until the shofar of Yovel on Yom Kippur drags him out like a lifeguard.

title.en: Beis Lechem, the place of Yovel

summary.en: The Rav calls Megillas Rus the megillah of Yovel and, following the triad of time, place and soul, argues that the place of Yovel is Beis Lechem. David HaMelech and Mashiach, who gathers Jews back, are neshamos of Yovel, and Rachel near Beis Lechem was promised the return.

title.en: Naomi brings Rus out of Moav

summary.en: The Rav explains that Naomi, wife of Elimelech, had the task of malchus, to bring back lost souls; she went to Moav, the opposite of Yovel, to draw out Rus. He then brings Boaz's words to Rus about dipping her bread in vinegar and the Gemara's reading that it hints at Menashe.

title.en: Menashe's teshuvah and Boaz's painful hint

summary.en: The Rav tells of Menashe's wickedness, his captivity in a heated pot, his teshuvah and Hashem digging a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod against the angels. He then asks why Boaz, bound by the prohibition of hurting with words, told Rus about this blemish in her line.

title.en: Menashe appears to Rav Ashi

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara's story of Rav Ashi, who called Menashe 'our friend', and Menashe appearing to him in a dream to ask where one cuts the bread at hamotzi. Rav Ashi taught the answer the next day, and the halacha passed into the Rambam, the Shulchan Aruch and every Jewish table.

title.en: Boaz's comfort and the angels' objection

summary.en: The Rav answers that Boaz was comforting Rus: even the rasha from her line would teach Klal Yisrael the halacha of hamotzi. He then asks why Hashem smuggled Menashe in rather than tell the angels they were wrong, and brings the Yerushalmi on who decides the sinner's fate.

title.en: Levels of Torah and the Mishnah's dispute

summary.en: The Rav explains that teshuvah answers what the Torah's plain level does not, because there are levels in the soul and in Torah, and every Jew must return to his root. Thus the Mishnah, that Menashe has no share, and the Gemara, that he does, are both true at different levels, and Hashem acts on a level the angels cannot grasp.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, Mashiach and the first yibum

summary.en: The Rav brings the law that a man sentenced abroad who flees to Eretz Yisrael is judged again, because a deeper level of judgment is revealed there; so Mashiach, a neshama of Yovel, brings close every Jew. He then turns to yibum as a tikkun of souls, from Yehuda and Tamar to Boaz and Rus.

title.en: Yibum as a tunnel; neshamos in bread

summary.en: The Rav calls yibum a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod and ties it to Mashiach. He compares the body's unseen digestion of bread to the hidden tikkun of a neshama in food, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that hunger exists because a soul is wrapped in the food.

title.en: Eating with kavanah and Menashe's lesson

summary.en: The Rav contrasts careless eating with washing, a bracha and kavanah that elevate the neshama in the bread. Baking is the last stage of the bread's tikkun, so the part baked first shows Hashem hurrying its tikkun; this was Menashe's message to Rav Ashi, that Hashem expedites the tikkun of malchus Beis David.

title.en: Preparing for Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav returns to Shavuos as a return to one's roots and notes that the Torah commands preparation, seven weeks of counting, only for Shavuos. He urges using the last week of Sefirah, even after wasted time.

catalogTitle: התבוננות בנפלאות התורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that even in a generation without open miracles, the endless depth of the Torah, which a child and the greatest gadol learn from the same Chumash and Gemara, is itself a wonder that proves it comes from Heaven, and that Hashem reveals Himself to whoever opens his eyes.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that in the generation before Moshiach one no longer sees the open wonders earlier generations saw, and the test is to believe without seeing. Yet whoever reflects can see wonders even now, above all in the Torah, which Dovid HaMelech asked to see and called sweeter than honey; one who does not taste it is like a sick patient who blames the food. He then contrasts a schoolchild's textbooks, replaced every year as he outgrows them, with the Chumash and Gemara that a child, a rosh yeshiva and the great Acharonim all learn, each seeing new things. The answer is that Torah comes from the Infinite and is itself endless, with four layers of PaRDeS, while a secular book ends at the page. Seeing this requires that Hashem open one's eyes, as with Hagar and the Chashmona'im's jar of oil. Finally, like Avraham Avinu who recognized the Owner of the lit palace, whoever strengthens his emunah will see Hashem's wonders in his daily life, for which Jews thank Him in Modim.

en: In this generation there are no open revelations, and the test is to believe without seeing; yet one who reflects can still see wonders that cry out that there is a Creator and that the Torah is true.
The Torah is sweet, and one who does not taste its sweetness has lost his sense of taste, like a sick patient who blames the hospital food.
Secular textbooks are outgrown and replaced every year, while the same Chumash and Gemara serve a child, a rosh yeshiva and the greatest Torah giants, each seeing new things in them.
Because the Torah comes from the Infinite, it is itself endless, with four layers of depth (pshat, remez, drush, sod), while a secular book ends at the page.
One can look at a thing and not see it until Hashem opens one's eyes, as with Hagar and the well and the Greeks who did not see the sealed jar of oil.
Everything that happens to a Jew, down to a single day, is full of wonders, and whoever strengthens his emunah will see Hashem revealing Himself through them.

candidateTopics: Avraham Avinu and the lit palace

title.en: Wonders hidden in our generation; the sweetness of Torah

summary.en: The Rav says that today one no longer sees open wonders and the test is to believe without seeing, but one who reflects can still see wonders, above all in the Torah. He brings Dovid HaMelech's request to see the wonders of the Torah and his praise of its sweetness, compares one who does not taste it to a sick patient who blames the food, and explains that both the Written and the Oral Torah are from Heaven.

title.en: Schoolbooks are outgrown; the Chumash and Gemara are not

summary.en: The Rav describes how an American child gets new, thicker textbooks every grade through college because the old ones become too elementary. A Jewish child, by contrast, keeps the same Chumash all his life, and the Bava Metzia he learned at nine he learns again at thirteen and eighteen as an entirely different study; it is the same Gemara learned by the great Acharonim and Rishonim, sealed by Ravina and Rav Ashi and given to Moshe Rabbeinu at Sinai.

title.en: Why the Torah never runs out: from the Infinite

summary.en: The Rav asks why a secular book must be replaced while a Chumash or Gemara can be learned again and again with new discoveries, and answers that the Torah comes from the Infinite and is therefore endless. No human could create a wisdom that is simple for a child and deep for a genius; this itself is a wonder. He explains the four layers of PaRDeS, noting that even later Amoraim lost the power of drush, and contrasts this with secular wisdom that is only surface.

title.en: Looking without seeing: Hagar and the jar of oil

summary.en: The Rav brings Hagar, who did not see the well beside her dying son until Hashem opened her eyes, and the Greeks who defiled all the oil in the Heichal but did not see the jar sealed by the Kohen Gadol. He says one who learns Torah honestly, davens well and guards himself from sin will have his eyes opened, and that not only the Torah but everything that happens to a Jew each day is full of wonders.

title.en: Avraham and the lit palace; daily miracles in Modim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash of a man who saw a lit palace in the wilderness until its owner revealed himself, applied to Avraham Avinu who saw the order of the world and history until Hashem revealed Himself to him. So too whoever strengthens his emunah and fear of Heaven will see Hashem in the wonders of his Torah and his day, and the Rav points to Modim, said three times daily, where Jews thank Hashem for His daily miracles.

catalogTitle: חנוכה - שורש החקירה מהיונים

oneLiner.en: The Rav traces philosophy back to the Greeks, who denied the natural instinct of emunah and replaced it with the worship of physical strength and beauty, and presents Chanukah as the fight against that substitute.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that the great Torah thinkers wrote works of chakirah (philosophical inquiry) only because Jewish intellectuals in Arab lands were drawn after gentile philosophy, whose root is Greek wisdom; the Torah itself never sets out to prove that there is a Creator. Citing the Bnei Yissaschar, he explains that one who 'tests' both sides is, for that moment, a kofer, and that the siddur puts Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu for this reason. Philosophy, he says, is mental acrobatics: like a chess champion, any philosopher can be refuted by a bigger mind. The Greeks set up reason as the only thing to believe, to throw off the yoke. But Hashem created an instinct of emunah in every person, just as He created appetite, and an instinct must be satisfied. So the Greeks made idols of physical strength and beauty, the root of sport and fashion. Chanukah, whose gematria equals guf, fought this. He closes by urging bochurim to make a cheshbon hanefesh.

en: The Torah never sets out to prove that there is a Creator; the Jewish works of chakirah were written only to counter gentile philosophy that attracted Jewish intellectuals.
Philosophy cannot reach absolute truth: whatever proofs one thinker brings, a greater mind can come and refute them.
Hashem created in every person an instinct of emunah, just as He created the appetite for food, because without trust neither personal nor social life could exist.
Having rejected emunah in G-d, the Greeks still had to satisfy that instinct, so they deified physical strength and beauty.
The Chashmona'im fought against these two substitutes for emunah, and the message of Chanukah is that victory comes not through might but through the spirit of Hashem.

title.en: Why Torah giants wrote works of chakirah

summary.en: The Rav recalls the earlier discussion of the Jewish philosophers led by the Rambam and the controversy over his books, notes that the Torah never tries to prove the Creator's existence, and explains that these works were needed because Jewish intellectuals in Arab lands were drawn after gentile philosophy rooted in Greek wisdom.

title.en: Testing both sides, and philosophy as mental acrobatics

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that one who weighs, in the philosophical way, whether there is a Ribono shel Olam is a kofer at that moment, and explains why the siddur says Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu. He then calls philosophy mental acrobatics and compares it to chess champions: any proof can be overturned by a greater mind.

title.en: Greek philosophy and the instinct of emunah

summary.en: The Rav traces philosophy to Greece and explains that its axiom, to believe only what reason proves, was a way to throw off the yoke. Against this he shows that Hashem created an instinct of emunah in every person, just like appetite, without which buying milk or asking a stranger the time would be impossible; the Greeks, whom the Chashmona'im fought, tried to nullify it.

title.en: Idols of strength and beauty

summary.en: The Rav explains that every instinct must be gratified, illustrating with what a psychologist told him about feeding through a zipper in the stomach. Since the Greeks would not believe in G-d, who would bind them, they made idols of physical strength and beauty; from this came the Olympics and athletics, and the hero-worship of athletes today.

title.en: Chanukah against the worship of the body

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chashmona'im fought with mesirus nefesh against the two substitutes for emunah, beauty and strength of the body, the worship of beauty showing also in designer clothing. Just as Moshiach equals nachash in gematria, Chanukah equals guf; the haftarah's 'not by might nor by strength but by My spirit' is its message, and the Greeks' idols in the Beis HaMikdash were what the victory removed.

title.en: Kelipas Yavan today and a Chanukah cheshbon hanefesh

summary.en: The Rav laments that the Greek kelipah of sports heroes and designer fashion has entered the batei medrash, explains with the Gemara's 'today he says do this' how it leads step by step toward avodah zarah, contrasts an elder who kept his wedding Shabbos garment all his life, and calls on bochurim to make a cheshbon hanefesh on Chanukah.

catalogTitle: אמונה של כלל ישראל תלוי במעמד הר סיני

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvah of emunah rests on the mesorah of Maamad Har Sinai, where Hashem spoke to an entire nation, unlike every other faith that rests on one individual.

abstract.en: The Rav asks what the halachos of the mitzvah of emunah are: just as a sukkah must be built according to its halachos, emunah, which the Rambam counts among the 613 mitzvos, has its own laws. The instinct of faith, contemplating nature and philosophical inquiry were discussed earlier; now he turns to the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah. First he gives the gist: something one individual reports can be doubted, but an event witnessed by multitudes cannot be denied, as with George Washington or Julius Caesar. Other religions rest on one man and his charisma or wonders, while the Torah was given before millions at Sinai and handed down by the whole people. He then learns the Rambam: Moshe was not believed because of his signs, which he performed for practical needs, but because of Sinai, where Hashem spoke face to face with the nation. A later navi is believed only because Moshe commanded it, as witnesses are believed by Hashem's command.

en: Emunah is one of the 613 mitzvos, so like every mitzvah it has halachos, and the Rambam sets them out in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah.
What one individual claims can be believed or doubted, but an event that happened before multitudes cannot be denied by any reasonable person.
Other religions rest on a single founder who swayed people with his character or wonders, while the Jewish people believe in no individual.
At Sinai Hashem revealed Himself to millions, who all heard Him directly and passed it down to their children; this mesorah of a whole people is unique.
According to the Rambam, Moshe Rabbeinu was not believed because of his signs, which he performed out of need, but because of Maamad Har Sinai.
A later navi, like witnesses in beis din, is believed not because of his wonders but because the Torah commands it; the mitzvah of emunah itself is the mesorah.

candidateTopics: mesorah as the basis of faith

title.en: The halachos of the mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: After a question on Rashi about the first mitzvah, the Rav asks what the halachos of emunah are, comparing it to a sukkah that must follow its halachos. He reviews the ways to emunah discussed earlier and turns to the Rambam, noting that in the Yad the Rambam speaks as halacha, unlike the Moreh Nevuchim.

title.en: A public event cannot be denied

summary.en: The Rav states that the Jewish emunah comes from Sinai and cannot be questioned, and sets out the rule: an individual's report may be doubted, but a public event may not. He illustrates with George Washington and Julius Caesar, whose existence and deeds no sane person denies even if many stories about them are false.

title.en: Other faiths rest on one man; Sinai on a nation

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Christianity and Islam, each founded on one individual who swayed people with charisma or wonders, with the Torah, given before millions at Har Sinai who all heard Hashem and passed it down. Even other religions accept the Torah because they cannot deny it, claiming only that it was later replaced.

title.en: The Rambam: not signs but Sinai

summary.en: The Rav learns the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8: belief based on signs leaves a doubt, and Moshe's wonders were done for practical needs. Belief in Moshe comes from Sinai, where the people saw with their own eyes and Hashem spoke 'face to face' with all of them, and no lie can be handed to later generations without protest.

title.en: Believing a navi, like believing witnesses

summary.en: The Rav explains that a later navi is believed not for his wonders but because Moshe commanded it, just as beis din believes two witnesses although they might lie, as in the case of Navos. He concludes that the other ways to emunah only support it, while the mitzvah itself is the mesorah, and says the Rambam will be continued next week.

catalogTitle: Preparing for שבועות through Torah and Mitzvos

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches children that just as the shofar of Yovel returns every slave to his land and family, the fiftieth day, Shavuos, returns every Yid to his roots and to Hashem, and he urges them to prepare for it with Torah and teshuvah.

abstract.en: Speaking to children preparing for Shavuos, the Rav first recalls the advice of a great mechanech, Rabbi Elias, never to be afraid of telling young boys something deep. He then explains that Hashem built laws into creation, like day and night or gravity, and that one such law is Yovel: everything must return to its source. Every Yid must return to Eretz Yisrael and to Hashem, which is the task of Mashiach and his shofar of freedom. Through the eved ivri of Parshas Mishpatim he contrasts the seventh year, when Hashem throws the drowning slave a rope, with the fiftieth year, when He dives in and pulls him out. Leaving Mitzrayim and counting seven times seven to Matan Torah follow the same pattern. Every Shavuos carries a scent of Yovel and a new Matan Torah, so the Rav urges the children to do teshuvah, learn with diligence and beg Hashem for the true Yovel of Mashiach.

en: Hashem placed laws into creation, and one of them is that everything must return to the place it came from.
Yovel is the return of every Yid to his roots: to Eretz Yisrael, to his family and to Hashem, which Mashiach will bring with his shofar of freedom.
In the seventh year Hashem only throws the slave a rope, but in the fiftieth year He dives in and pulls him out whether he wants or not.
After Yetzias Mitzrayim the Yidden counted seven times seven, and the fiftieth day, like the fiftieth year, was Matan Torah with the sound of the shofar.
Every Shavuos there is a new Matan Torah and a reminder of Yovel; even one who cannot hear the shofar with his ears can hear it with his heart.
Shavuos must be prepared for, through Sefirah, teshuvah and the days of preparation, in order to receive one's portion in the Torah.

laws of nature as Hashem's laws

title.en: Something deep, and the laws of creation

summary.en: The Rav tells the children that all success in Torah comes from Shavuos, recalls Rabbi Elias's advice not to fear telling young boys something deep, and begins with the laws Hashem built into nature: day and night, summer and winter, and the apple that falls to the ground.

title.en: Yovel: every Yid returns to his source

summary.en: The Rav explains Yovel as a law of creation: as the apple returns to the ground, every Yid must return to Eretz Yisrael and to Hashem. This is the work of Mashiach, as the Rambam writes, and his shofar will proclaim freedom from the yetzer hara and return us to the state of Adam before the sin.

title.en: The rope and the lifeguard

summary.en: Through the eved ivri of Parshas Mishpatim, who loses his freedom and his place in the Jewish family, the Rav contrasts the seventh year, when Hashem throws him a rope he may refuse, with Yovel, when Hashem dives in and pulls him out. He then applies the pattern to Mitzrayim, the counting of seven times seven and the shofar of Matan Torah.

title.en: Every Shavuos, a taste of Yovel

summary.en: The Rav says Mashiach can come any day, and illustrates with a spinning penny that the chance stays even no matter how long we have waited. Even without Mashiach, every Shavuos carries a scent of Yovel and a new Matan Torah, and the shofar that cannot be heard with the ears can be heard with the heart.

title.en: Teshuvah and preparing for Matan Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the Yidden arrived at Sinai with teshuvah, and says that this teshuvah returns every Rosh Chodesh Sivan. The Torah commands preparing for Shavuos through Sefirah and the days of preparation, so he urges the children to learn with diligence and kavanah, do teshuvah and beg Hashem, and closes with a tefillah for the shofar of Mashiach.

catalogTitle: האומות מכירים וכופרים מטעם של rationalization

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains from the Rambam that our belief in the Torah rests on the mesorah of Har Sinai, so no later prophet can change it, and that the nations, who know this, deny it through rationalization born of jealousy.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that the mesorah of Klal Yisroel is true because a whole nation heard Hashem at Har Sinai, and that a prophet is believed only because the Torah commands it, like two witnesses. With the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah he shows that a prophet with signs who contradicts Moshe is not heeded, as witnesses who say it is night are not believed by one who sees daylight. The Torah cannot be added to or changed, so the claims of the nations about a new law collapse; Bilaam himself said Hashem does not change His mind. Why do they hold on? Rationalization and jealousy of the chosen people. The Rav applies this to Rashi's question about the first mitzvah, to Moshe as father of all prophets, and to the world's preoccupation with Jews and Yerushalayim. A story of a dying heretic who recanted shows that rationalization falls away at the end. He closes that mesorah is the halachic basis of emunah.

en: Belief in a prophet after Moshe is only a decree of the Torah, like believing two witnesses, while belief in Moshe rests on what the whole nation saw at Har Sinai.
A prophet who comes with wonders to contradict Moshe is not heeded, just as a court that sees daylight does not believe witnesses who say it is night.
The Torah cannot be added to, reduced or exchanged, so any claim that Hashem gave a new Torah is false by the very Torah its claimants accept.
The nations hold on to their claims through rationalization, driven above all by jealousy of the Jewish people as the chosen nation.
Even mitzvos given to Avraham and the Avos are kept only because Moshe wrote them in the Torah; Moshe is the father of the prophets before him and after him.
Mesorah, not philosophy, is the halachic basis of emunah, and it is the strongest of the ways to faith.

title.en: The mesorah of Sinai and belief in a prophet

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the mesorah is true because the whole nation heard Hashem at Sinai and passed it down. He explains from the Rambam that a later prophet is believed only by decree of the Torah, like two witnesses, which is not true knowledge.

title.en: No prophet can change the Torah

summary.en: The Rav reads the Rambam that a prophet who performs wonders to contradict Moshe is not heeded, comparing him to witnesses who claim it is night in daylight. He continues with the Rambam that the Torah can never be changed, rejecting the claims that Hashem gave a new law or moved Shabbos to Sunday or Friday.

title.en: Bilaam's words and the nations' jealousy

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk said by Bilaam, that Hashem is not a man who changes His mind, and shows that the nations' whole structure collapses on the Torah they themselves accept. He explains that they hold on through rationalization, driven by jealousy of the chosen people, as the Ohr HaChaim writes on Yosef's brothers.

title.en: Why HaChodesh is the first mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav asks on Rashi's opening why 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem' is called the first mitzvah when earlier mitzvos were given. Following the Rambam, he answers that an individual prophet like Avraham cannot be believed with certainty; we keep even milah only because Moshe wrote it, so HaChodesh is the first mitzvah received from Moshe, who is father of the prophets before and after him.

title.en: Mesorah as halacha; the world revolves around Jews

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Rambam's Yad HaChazakah is a book of halacha, not philosophy, and its basis for emunah is the mesorah of Sinai. The nations are jealous and know the truth subconsciously: everything revolves around the Jews, Eretz Yisroel and Yerushalayim, yet they deceive themselves, as the Kotzker said.

title.en: The heretic who recanted; mesorah as the strongest way

summary.en: The Rav retells a story of a leading heretic in Eretz Yisroel who on his deathbed told his students that the Torah is true, and explains that at death rationalization falls away. He then sums up the ways to emunah discussed so far and closes that mesorah is the halachic and strongest way, tied to yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah.

catalogTitle: עיקר האמונה - אמונה פשוטה

oneLiner.en: Through the Spanish expulsion and the Ohr HaChaim of Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz, the Rav shows that what keeps a Jew in his faith is not philosophy but simple emunah received by mesorah, the faith on which Chavakuk founded all the mitzvos.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that Jewish faith rests on mesorah, passed from parents and teachers back to Har Sinai, and that simple faith, not proofs, is what holds. He brings Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz, who lived through the expulsion from Spain, which fell on Tisha B'Av, a day of calamities from the spies through Beitar. Yaavetz asks why the decree came, and notes that the philosophers who had proven Hashem's truth by logic converted outwardly, while simple people left Spain with mesirus nefesh. The Rav then describes the controversy over the Rambam's works, the burning of the Gemara in Paris, and, in a tangent, how copying errors in the Gemara were corrected. Rabbeinu Yonah saw the burning as a punishment and did teshuvah, producing Shaarei Teshuvah. Chavakuk founded all mitzvos on emunah. Finally the Rav notes that each person, and each period of a great man's life such as the Chazon Ish's, has its own focus.

en: Jewish faith is built on mesorah, received from parents and teachers generation after generation back to Har Sinai, not on philosophical proofs.
In the Spanish expulsion the philosophers who had proven Hashem's truth outwardly converted, while simple Jews left with mesirus nefesh.
What holds a Jew to emunah is knowing that he comes from a people who have given their lives for Hashem since Avraham Avinu.
Rabbeinu Yonah saw the burning of the Gemara as a heavenly punishment for encouraging the burning of the Rambam's works, did teshuvah, and from this came Shaarei Teshuvah.
Chavakuk founded all the mitzvos on emunah because later generations can no longer exert themselves equally in every mitzvah.
Each person, even among the upright, puts more of his strength into particular areas, and great people change their focus over the course of their lives.

title.en: Faith by mesorah, and the decree of Spain

summary.en: The Rav recalls that emunah rests on mesorah from Har Sinai and that simple faith, not proofs, is what endures. He introduces Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz and his Ohr HaChaim, written in the time of the Spanish expulsion, and describes the decree to convert or leave Spain with nothing, and the Inquisition.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, the expulsion, and the Yaavetz's lesson

summary.en: The Rav tells how the expulsion fell on Tisha B'Av, a day of calamities from the spies through Beitar, and how the exiles left to music and wandered destitute. He brings the Yaavetz's reckoning of why it happened, and his observation that the philosophers converted while simple Jews held firm, concluding that only simple emunah, received by mesorah from Yetzias Mitzrayim and Har Sinai, keeps a Jew.

title.en: The Rambam controversy and the burning in Paris

summary.en: The Rav describes the opposition of the Ashkenazi gedolim to the Rambam's path of chakirah, the burning of his works in Paris, and the later decree that burned wagonloads of handwritten Gemaras. He explains that copying by hand caused errors, which is why Tosafos sometimes dispute Rashi's girsa, and how the Baalei Tosafos corrected the text.

title.en: Printing and the correct girsa of the Gemara

summary.en: In a digression the Rav explains how the gedolim, chiefly the Bach, corrected the printed Gemara, why remaining differences of girsa between Rashi and Tosafos are both true, and why masechtos that were rarely learned, such as Nedarim, Nazir and Kodashim, still have many errors noted by the Shitah Mekubetzes.

title.en: Rabbeinu Yonah's teshuvah and Chavakuk's one mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav tells that after the Gemaras were burned in Paris, Rabbeinu Yonah, who had encouraged burning the Rambam's works, saw it as a heavenly punishment and did teshuvah, which brought about Shaarei Teshuvah. He then brings the Gemara in Makkos that Chavakuk founded all the mitzvos on one, emunah, explaining that smaller generations cannot exert themselves equally in everything.

title.en: Each person's own focus; the Chazon Ish

summary.en: The Rav observes that every person puts more strength into certain areas, Torah, tefillah or tzedakah, and that great people change their focus over their lives. He describes the Chazon Ish, hidden and learning in Vilna, and later in Bnei Brak spending hours daily on people's needs and on yeshivos, and asks where such differences come from, leaving the answer for the next shiur.
